labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

An OAuth-connected personal developer-mode MCP 2.0 plugin exposes a custom event successfully. Authenticated tools work, but both Chat and Work conversations report no native event-subscription action.

A controlled Work retry successfully called an authenticated health-check tool, then reported: "this Work chat exposes no native MCP event subscription action or callable events/subscribe method. No subscription attempt was made". No subscription was stored or callback verified.

This is an integration failure with root cause unknown, not a confirmed defect in a particular public code path.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Connect an OAuth-authenticated personal developer-mode MCP plugin using protocol 2026-07-28, advertising tools and events through server/discover and providing authenticated events/list, events/subscribe and events/unsubscribe.
2. Refresh the plugin. Confirm that its Events section displays the custom event and authenticated read tools succeed.
3. Select the plugin in a new Work conversation and request: "Subscribe to item.updated for collection demo. Notify me when an item changes. Do not poll or perform writes."
4. Observe that the conversation reports no native subscription action and does not create a subscription. The same result was observed in Chat mode.

Event/filter names above are neutral substitutions for privacy, not a separately deployed sample. A controlled retry maintained successful local and public HTTPS metadata checks throughout and successfully called an authenticated tool. Server state showed zero accepted subscriptions or callback verifications; no complete HTTP request trace was captured, so aggregate state alone cannot exclude an early rejected request.

### What is the expected behavior?

ChatGPT should initiate the documented native MCP event subscription lifecycle after successful event discovery, or explain the specific account, mode, rollout or configuration requirement preventing it.

### Additional information

Hosted ChatGPT Work; hosted version is not exposed.

Official documentation: https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/mcp-events
Announcement: https://openai.com/index/devday-2026-recap/

PR #37494 adds relevant hosted-app event discovery/subscription infrastructure. Its internal events/stream path differs from the documented external webhook events/subscribe interface; no justified upstream patch or confirmed root cause was identified.

I searched existing reports and did not find an exact match. Which supported path registers conversation subscriptions when plugin event discovery succeeds? If this belongs to a hosted registry or another component rather than this repository, please route it appropriately.

Project purpose, deployed identifiers, account details, endpoints and private logs are intentionally omitted.

issues.body:
### What version of the IDE extension are you using?

`openai.chatgpt 26.1007.21434`, win32-x64, stable. Bundled Codex: `0.162.0-alpha.17.2`.
Stable extension version checked against VS Code Marketplace on 2026-10-15.

### What subscription do you have?

Signed in with ChatGPT. The subscription tier was not collected for this report.

### Which IDE are you using?

Visual Studio Code 1.141.2.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 x64, build 26200.

### What issue are you seeing?

The extension sidebar loads and a minimal text-only prompt receives a response, but background requests and diagnostics still report errors:

1. During the successful chat test, `/subscriptions` returned HTTP 403 with `errorCode=cloudflare_challenge`. Earlier `/accounts/optimized/check` did the same. Reloading the VS Code window did not eliminate this background failure.
2. `fs/getMetadata` logs `os error 2` / `os error 3` without the requested paths. The selected project's seven relevant editor files exist.
3. `turn-diff-capture-start` logs `failureReason=output_limit`, stdout limit `1048576` bytes and `stdoutBytes=6549504`, for a large dirty repository. Git shortstat succeeds for the same comparison.
4. `codex doctor` reports history-pointer discrepancies despite healthy SQLite databases and already-paginated history.

These symptoms may have independent causes. No causal link between the history warnings and missing-path errors is established.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed on this existing installation on 2026-10-15; a deterministic clean-install reproduction is not established:

1. Open the Codex sidebar in VS Code with the existing ChatGPT sign-in.
2. Reload the VS Code window and open a new text chat.
3. Send a minimal prompt requesting only a short confirmation, with no file reading or modifications.
4. Observe that the response arrives, while the Codex output log records the background failures above.
5. Run the bundled `codex doctor --summary --no-color --ascii` and inspect the detailed report.
6. For the affected history IDs, run `codex migrate-rollouts --thread <affected-id> --json` **without `--apply`**: all three representations inspected report `already_paginated`, `bytes_processed=0`.

### What is the expected behavior?

Background account/subscription requests should succeed or provide an actionable supported recovery flow. Missing-path diagnostics should identify the relevant path safely. Existing migrated history should have consistent pointers, or a supported repair procedure should be documented.

Please clarify whether the 1 MiB turn-diff capture limit has a supported configuration or workaround that does not require committing, hiding or deleting working files.

### Additional information

Diagnostics performed:

- `codex doctor`: **19 ok, 1 idle, 6 notes, 5 warn, 0 fail; degraded**.
- Login status: `Logged in using ChatGPT`.
- WebSocket handshake: HTTP 101; assets CDN: HTTP 200.
- Inspected Codex SQLite databases pass integrity checks.
- Doctor reports 2 missing active database rows, 1 stale row and 1 duplicate rollout thread ID involving old compressed history.
- The referenced compressed files exist. Read-only migration inspection reports already-paginated history as described above.
- No authentication reset, database editing, history deletion, security changes or migration application was performed.
- Working files were not committed, hidden or deleted to suppress the Git-output warning.

Questions for maintainers:

- Is the subscription Cloudflare challenge a known issue for this extension build?
- Is there a supported repair for stale pointers to already-paginated history?
- How can `fs/getMetadata` safely report the specific failing path?
- Is the 1 MiB turn-diff capture limit configurable through a supported setting?

Possibly related reports: #49351 (also mentions subscription/account-check 403s, but primarily concerns dictation), #50403 (mentions missing-path errors, but primarily concerns queued-message failures). This report does not claim a dictation or queued-message failure.

Only sanitized diagnostic facts are included. No account IDs, email, thread IDs, project name, local user paths, tokens, session content, source files or raw logs are attached.

issues.body: ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)? 26.1007.71326 ### What subscription do you have? pro ### What platform is your computer? Windows 11 x64 + WSL2 ### What issue are you seeing? ### Summary On October 15, 2026, Codex Desktop blocked the final response of a legitimate, owner-authorized C source-code refactoring and regression-testing task with a cybersecurity safety warning. The task involved no external target, offensive security activity, unauthorized access, or exploit development. The interruption occurred after approximately 8 minutes and 52 seconds of productive execution, during or after local regression-test activity. **Environment** - Product: Codex Desktop on Windows, using WSL2 - Model: GPT-6.1 Sol, Extra High reasoning - Toolchain: CMake, MinGW-w64, Python, GCC, ASan/UBSan ### Requested work I asked Codex to maintain a legacy C application I wrote during my first year at university. The application has approximately 2,903 lines of C code and includes linked-list operations, file scanning, JSON output, and legacy AES/RSA functionality. The requirements were: 1. Preserve the original project completely, without modifying its files. 2. Create an independent working copy. 3. Split the monolithic C source into compilation units. 4. Introduce CMake-based builds. 5. Identify and document existing defects, without fixing them. 6. Preserve legacy behavior for subsequent independent auditing. 7. Use my local WSL toolchain, with explicit permission to execute outside the Codex sandbox when necessary. This was a software-maintenance and reproducibility task, not a request to weaponize any discovered defects. ### Observed behavior Codex reported successful progress: - Created and hash-verified an independent snapshot of eight original files. - Split 51 functions into 16 C modules. - Preserved the original source content and generated a source-line mapping. - Successfully built a Windows executable through CMake and MinGW under WSL. - Completed three checks on a Linux core build with ASan/UBSan enabled. - Preserved existing compiler warnings. - Identified suspected linked-list defects for later documentation. Codex explicitly avoided running the original program entry point containing file-deletion and PHP-invocation logic. It then began checking behavioral equivalence and reproducing existing defects using temporary test data. The last visible activity included execution of `tools/run_probes.py` in Windows and WSL environments. Instead of delivering the requested results, the UI displayed: **"无法显示此内容"** ("This content can't be shown") The localized message stated that extra caution was being applied to cybersecurity requests and suggested Daybreak access. The UI did not identify any specific unsafe operation, prohibited request, or triggering content. ### Impact The safety intervention prevented delivery of the final audit results, defect locations, reproduction conditions, and build instructions, despite the preceding successful development work. The distinction matters: discovering a memory-safety defect, preserving it for an audit, and testing its behavior with ASan/UBSan are normal software-engineering activities. None of those actions inherently requests offensive exploitation. This appears to be a false-positive cybersecurity classification, although the precise triggering operation or output has not been established. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? Feedback ID: 01a13d43-fa94-7631-8f40-75b1cfd70589 ### What is the expected behavior? Codex should complete legitimate, owner-authorized source-code maintenance, CMake migration, memory-safety diagnostics, and regression testing without incorrectly triggering cybersecurity restrictions. Specifically, Codex should: 1. Preserve the original source tree and existing bugs as requested. 2. Complete the CMake migration and behavioral-equivalence checks. 3. Report identified memory-safety defects, their triggering conditions, and reproduction evidence. 4. Deliver the final report and artifact locations without suppressing the entire response. If a specific operation genuinely violates a safety restriction, Codex should distinguish that operation from the surrounding legitimate development work and preserve access to non-restricted results. Ordinary ASan/UBSan debugging and documentation of existing C memory errors should not require offensive-security authorization. ### Additional information ### Possible recurring failure mode This is the second similar interruption I experienced within approximately 24 hours. **October 14, 2026:** Codex encountered a cybersecurity-related interruption during dynamic verification of my own C-based ternary virtual machine. The testing included invalid instruction encodings, bounds checking, ASan/UBSan diagnostics, and reproduction of memory-safety defects. **October 15, 2026:** Codex encountered another cybersecurity restriction while refactoring my independent legacy C file-classification project and performing local regression tests. ASan/UBSan were again involved. The two projects have different functionality, but both involve authorized memory-safety testing of locally owned code. I suspect that sanitizer-related diagnostics, bug reproduction, or subsequent defect-analysis output may be correlated with these false positives. **This is a hypothesis, not an established root cause.** The available evidence does not establish whether the original prompt, tool output, generated analysis, or a downstream safety check triggered either block. ### Diagnostic information - October 15 feedback ID: `01a13d43-fa94-7631-8f40-75b1cfd70589` - Model: GPT-6.1 Sol, Extra High reasoning - Environment: Codex Desktop, Windows, WSL2 - Incident time zone: UTC+08:00 ### Related reports - #42955 — Authorized C++ gtest/ASAN regression testing blocked. - #48791 — Suspected cybersecurity false positive after a local FFmpeg decoder audit. - #52818 — Authorized local source review blocked and redirected toward Daybreak. These reports appear related at the symptom level, but they are not proven to share the same underlying cause. ### Additional reproduction details The following sequence was observed: 1. Codex was asked to refactor an owner-controlled legacy C project without modifying the original source or fixing existing bugs. 2. CMake/MinGW builds succeeded under WSL2. 3. The Linux core build passed three checks with ASan/UBSan enabled. 4. Local regression probes completed, including the reported result: `PASS: 5 known-bug repros confirmed on disposable fixtures`. 5. The final response was suppressed by a cybersecurity safety warning. This sequence is documented in the attached screenshots. Deterministic reproduction in a fresh session has not yet been established. ### Requested investigation Please correlate the feedback ID with the affected Codex execution and identify which safety-check stage rejected the task. In particular, please investigate whether ordinary sanitizer diagnostics and memory-defect analysis are being misclassified as offensive cybersecurity activity. I am reporting this to help identify and correct a potential classification or output-handling defect, not to request removal of legitimate safety restrictions.

issues.body:
Codex inside the ChatGPT Windows desktop app fails immediately with “Unable to load organization settings” and stops before the Codex composer loads. Because the composer never appears, no desktop Codex session is created and I cannot type / to submit feedback or obtain a desktop session ID.
**Environment**  
- OS: Windows 11  
- ChatGPT Windows Desktop (MSIX/AppX) version: 26.924.1866.0  
- Codex CLI present on system: 0.158.0-alpha.2  
- Auth: ChatGPT OAuth

**Steps to reproduce**  
1. Launch ChatGPT Windows desktop app  
2. Sign in successfully  
3. Open Codex  
4. Immediately see dialog: “Unable to load organization settings” (Retry / Sign out / Exit)  
5. Retry repeats indefinitely

**Expected**  
Codex loads and shows the composer.

**Actual**  
Codex stops at organization-settings initialization; composer never renders; no desktop session is created.

**Comparison (same account)**  
- Web: https://chatgpt.com/codex works normally  
- CLI: logged in via ChatGPT and model requests succeed (returns OK)  
- codex doctor: auth/config/HTTP/WebSocket connectivity all OK (incl. successful WS handshake)

This appears isolated to the Codex integration in the ChatGPT Windows desktop app (desktop-specific org-settings fetch/init path).

**Troubleshooting performed**  
- Windows app Reset + full reinstall  
- Re-authenticated (fresh %USERPROFILE%\.codex\auth.json created)  
- Verified no proxy / WinHTTP proxy  
- Removed stale .codex junction from older migration; removed old switcher config  
- Confirmed no local policy/config files exist:  
  - %USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml (absent)  
  - %USERPROFILE%\.codex\managed_config.toml (absent)  
  - %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml (absent)  
- %USERPROFILE%\.codex\sessions contains only CLI sessions (originator: codex_exec); archived_sessions empty (no desktop session is created)

**Request**  
Please advise how to collect Windows desktop app logs/telemetry for this failure mode (when Codex UI fails before session creation), or investigate the desktop org-settings initialization/loading path.

**Attachments**  
Screenshot of the “Unable to load organization settings” dialog available on request.

Preserve ChatGPT authentication for Gov MCP servers

MCP servers at `https://gov.chatgpt.com` were treated as untrusted for ChatGPT authentication and switched to OAuth, preventing local Gov Apps from retaining the ChatGPT auth provider.

Trust the `https://gov.chatgpt.com` origin alongside the existing ChatGPT origin when resolving MCP server authentication. Origin matching preserves scheme, host, and port restrictions.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for Gov Apps URL construction, trusted origin normalization, rejection of lookalike hosts and nonstandard schemes or ports, and retention of the local ChatGPT auth provider. Verify that explicit OAuth servers and servers in remote environments do not receive the host provider.

prs.title: Reload the model catalog after account changes
prs.body:
Reload the model catalog after account changes

## Why

The app server retained its startup model provider for catalog requests, so signing in or out could leave `model/list` using stale provider settings or requiring a restart after managed provider requirements changed.

## What changed

- Invalidate the catalog after successful login and logout, then reload the effective configuration on the next model list or background refresh. Rebuild the models manager when the provider or catalog changes, while preserving existing threads' routes.
- Retain the original project context and the TUI's `--oss` provider selection across reloads. Retry configuration loading after falling back to defaults so temporary failures do not pin the fallback catalog.
- Keep provider policy checks for cached catalogs and apply runtime `api_key_model_discovery` toggles to the active catalog manager.

## Testing

Add and extend tests for provider selection and definition changes after login, catalog reloads after logout, OAuth gateway transitions, fallback recovery, project context, and runtime model discovery toggles.

prs.body:
Allow stdin review under active grants with sandbox prompts disabled

## Why

With granular sandbox approvals disabled, `write_stdin` rejected input to terminals retaining additional permissions even when those permissions were still granted.

## What changed

Let input reach approval review when the terminal's retained permissions match active grants for its environment. Require identical filesystem grants, including entry order, and an active network grant when retained permissions enable network access. Each input still requires review.

Keep rejecting input when retained authority is no longer covered or the approval policy changes to `Never`.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for user and Guardian review, turn grant expiry, session grants, and switching to `Never`. Cover filesystem restrictions, protected metadata, symlinks, and ordered denials, and verify that rejected input never reaches the terminal.

prs.title: Report terminal completion states and blocking reasons
prs.body:
Report terminal completion states and blocking reasons

## Why

Terminal status previously collapsed completed and failed turns into `idle` and reported blocking prompts without a reason. Blocking detection also depended on terminal title settings.

## What changed

- Emit `done` and `error` through OSC 7501 for live turn results, retaining them until deliberate keyboard, paste, or mouse input acknowledges them. Mouse movement does not acknowledge results.
- Classify blocking requests with `kind=permission`, `kind=question`, or `kind=auth`, including requests hidden behind another view or delayed while typing, independently of terminal title settings.
- Keep pending follow-up work and active goals `working`. Treat interrupted turns and replayed results as `idle` rather than new results.
- Preserve the existing iTerm2 OSC 21337 labels and indicators, mapping `done` and `error` to `Idle`.

## Testing

Add lifecycle and input-acknowledgment tests covering approvals, completion, failure, interruption, replay, pending follow-ups, and active goals. Extend blocking-request assertions and terminal protocol snapshots for the new states and reasons.

issues.title: Assess the impact of AST-aware file reads, search, and mapping

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: kind/customer-issue
labels.description: Issues that were reported by customers

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

labels.name: priority/p1
labels.description: Important and should be addressed in the near term.

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text

line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."

Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

issues.title: /compress command is not persistent across session resume

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only

labels.description: 1 day or less: trivial logic, UI adjustments, docs

issues.body:
### What happened?

The `/compress` command, which summarizes chat history to save tokens, is not persistent across session exits and resumes. When a user runs `/compress`, the in-memory chat history is correctly replaced by a summary, but this change is not written back to the session file on disk. Consequently, when the session is resumed later (using `--resume` or `/resume`), the CLI loads the original, uncompressed history from the session file, effectively losing the compression.

**Repro Steps:**
1. Start a chat with `gemini`.
2. Build up some history with several messages.
3. Run `/compress` and wait for completion.
4. Exit the CLI.
5. Resume the session with `gemini --resume latest`.
6. Observe that the history has reverted to its uncompressed state.

### What did you expect to happen?

Running `/compress` should persist the compressed history (the summary) to the session file on disk so that subsequent resumes of the same session correctly load the compressed state.

### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

OS: darwin (macOS)
Version: Current (detected in local development)

</details>

### Login information

N/A (General bug in persistence logic)

### Anything else we need to know?

Investigation shows that in `packages/core/src/core/client.ts`, the `tryCompressChat` method correctly replaces the `this.chat` object with a new `GeminiChat` initialized with the compressed history:
```typescript
this.chat = await this.startChat(newHistory, resumedData);
```
However, the `ChatRecordingService` (which manages the session file) is initialized with `resumedData` (which points to the existing session file) but is not explicitly instructed to overwrite the file's message history with the new `newHistory`. The `initialize` method in `ChatRecordingService` merely points to the existing file without clearing or updating its messages.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(cli): verify active binary update to prevent PATH shadowing false success
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an issue where `handleAutoUpdate` reported a successful update even when the active executing binary was shadowed in `$PATH` or targeted by a non-matching package manager prefix, leaving the user running the outdated binary.

## Details

- **Problem:** When multiple installations exist on a system (e.g., `/usr/local/bin` preceding `/usr/bin` in `$PATH`, or switched npm/pnpm global prefixes), running the global update command installs the new version into the package manager's prefix directory while the active binary executing Gemini CLI remains untouched. `handleAutoUpdate` previously relied solely on the update process exiting with code `0`, falsely emitting `update-success` ("Update successful! The new version will be used on your next run.") and causing an infinite update prompt loop on subsequent runs.
- **Solution:** Added post-update verification in `handleAutoUpdate`. When the child process exits with code `0`, `handleAutoUpdate` inspects the active running binary via `process.argv[1]` and checks its `package.json` version using `getPackageJson`.
  - If the active binary's version is verified to still be older than `info.update.latest`, `handleAutoUpdate` emits `update-failed` with a descriptive message explaining that the active binary was not updated and may be shadowed by another installation in `$PATH`.
  - Employs a fail-safe fallback: if `package.json` cannot be determined or if an error occurs during verification, it does not block legitimate updates.
  - Added optional `getPackageJsonFn` injection to `handleAutoUpdate` for robust, deterministic unit testing.

## Related Issues

Fixes #21553

## How to Validate

1. **Automated Unit Tests:**
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/utils/handleAutoUpdate.test.ts
   ```
   All tests pass, including new coverage for PATH shadowing detection and graceful fallback handling.

2. **Full Workspace Build & Tests:**
   ```bash
   npm run build
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli
   npm run lint
   npm run typecheck
   ```

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [ ] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [ ] Noted breaking changes (if any)
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [ ] MacOS
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
    - [ ] Podman
    - [ ] Seatbelt
  - [ ] Windows
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
  - [x] Linux
    - [x] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker

prs.title: fix(cli): resolve settings placeholders after loading .env files
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a load-order defect in `loadSettings()`: settings files were parsed,
expanded against `process.env`, and validated **before** `loadEnvironment()`
injected the variables from `.env` files. Any placeholder whose variable was
defined only in a `.env` file (for example
`"Authorization": "Bearer $GITHUB_MCP_PAT"`) stayed unexpanded, and the literal
string was sent to MCP servers (`400 Bad Format Authorization Header`).

Settings are now read once and resolved **after** `.env` files have been loaded,
so `.env` can be used to keep secrets out of version-controlled `settings.json`,
as the documentation already describes.

## Details

`.env` discovery cannot simply be moved earlier because it depends on settings
itself (`security.folderTrust.enabled`, `advanced.ignoreLocalEnv`,
`advanced.excludedEnvVars`, `tools.sandbox`, `security.auth.selectedType`).
The fix therefore keeps a single read of each file and performs two resolution
passes over the raw data inside `_doLoadSettings` (`packages/cli/src/config/settings.ts`):

1. **Read:** `load()` now only reads and parses JSON (fatal parse errors are
   still recorded here).
2. **Preliminary pass:** `resolve()` expands placeholders against the *shell*
   environment and validates/coerces. These settings feed the workspace trust
   check and `loadEnvironment()` exactly as before, so no security-relevant
   decision changes (this addresses the concern raised by the review bot on the
   earlier community attempt, #28597, which passed raw unexpanded settings into
   those checks).
3. **`loadEnvironment()`** populates `process.env` from the `.env` file.
4. **Final pass:** `resolve()` runs again with `.env` variables available. Only
   this pass records Zod validation warnings, so a `"$VAR"` that becomes valid
   after `.env` loading no longer produces a spurious "expected number, received
   string" warning, and nothing is reported twice.

Other notes:

- `originalSettings` (what gets persisted on save) still holds the unexpanded
  placeholders, so secrets are never written back to disk.
- `GEMINI_CLI_AUTH_OVERRIDE` is now applied once to the raw user settings
  (before cloning into `originalSettings`) instead of separately to both
  objects; observable behaviour is unchanged and it remains visible to
  `loadEnvironment()` for the Cloud Shell / Vertex AI case.
- The legacy theme-name mapping moved after the final pass; it doesn't influence
  trust or `.env` loading.
- Startup cost: each settings file is expanded and validated twice. Files are
  small and `loadSettings()` is cached, so this is negligible.
- Known, inherent limitation (now documented in code and docs): settings that
  control `.env` loading can only reference shell variables, never `.env` ones.
- One existing `eslint-disable` comment became unnecessary and was removed; no
  new ones were added.

## Related Issues

Fixes #28684

## How to Validate

### Automated Unit Tests

Unit tests (exercise the real `_doLoadSettings` pipeline with only `fs`
mocked; `dotenv` parsing is real):

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/config/settings.test.ts
```

The new `describe('resolving settings placeholders from .env files')` block
contains 7 tests. Before this fix, the resolution tests fail with the exact
symptom from the issue:

```diff
- "Authorization": "Bearer ghp_secretTokenHere"
+ "Authorization": "Bearer $GITHUB_MCP_PAT"
```

The remaining tests are regression guards: placeholders stay unexpanded in
`originalSettings`, shell variables win over `.env`, a `.env` in an untrusted
workspace is still ignored, the trust check still receives settings that were
resolved and coerced from the shell environment, and no duplicate Zod validation
warnings are emitted across the two passes.

### Manual End-to-End Verification

1. **Create `.env` in the repository root** (ensure `GITHUB_MCP_PAT` is **not** exported in your shell: `unset GITHUB_MCP_PAT`):
   ```env
   GITHUB_MCP_PAT=some-token
   ```
   *(If connecting directly to `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/`, use a valid GitHub PAT here.)*

2. **Add `mcpServers` to `.gemini/settings.json` in the repository root:**
   ```json
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "github": {
         "httpUrl": "https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/",
         "headers": {
           "Authorization": "Bearer $GITHUB_MCP_PAT"
         }
       }
     }
   }
   ```
   > **Tip (testing with dummy `some-token` without a real GitHub PAT):** Set `"httpUrl": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp/"` and run `nc -l 8787` in a second terminal to inspect the raw incoming HTTP headers.

3. **Build and start Gemini CLI from the repository root:**
   ```bash
   npm i
   npm run build
   npm run start
   ```
   *(If prompted to trust the workspace folder on startup, select **Trust folder**.)*

4. **Verify:**
   - **With `https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/` and a valid PAT:** Run `/mcp` inside Gemini CLI. `github` connects (`🟢 github - Ready`) instead of failing with `401 Unauthorized` / `400 Bad Format Authorization Header`.
   - **With `nc -l 8787` and dummy `some-token`:** Observe the raw HTTP request in the `nc` terminal:
     ```http
     POST /mcp/ HTTP/1.1
     ...
     authorization: Bearer some-token
     ```
     confirming `Bearer some-token` is sent instead of the literal `Bearer $GITHUB_MCP_PAT`.

5. **Clean up local test files:**
   ```bash
   rm .env
   git checkout -- .gemini/settings.json
   ```

`npm run preflight` passes locally.

prs.title: fix(core): replace fuzzy requestedExplicitly logic with glob matching in read-many-files
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes a critical context-bloat bug (b/561554390 / #29045) in `read-many-files` where binary assets (images, PDFs, audio) were incorrectly treated as "explicitly requested" due to naive `String.prototype.includes()` fuzzy substring matching on file stems and extensions, causing inadvertent base64 inlining.

## Details

- **Glob-Based Pattern Evaluation**: Replaced raw string substring matching with `isAssetExplicitlyRequested()` utilizing the repository's standard glob library (`picomatch`, zero new dependencies).
- **Strict Differentiation**: Broad wildcard patterns and directory traversals (e.g., `*`, `**/*`, `src/**`, `**/*report*/**`, `assets/*`) no longer trigger explicit binary inlining. An asset is only treated as explicitly requested if an include pattern matches the file AND explicitly targets either:
      1. **A specific extension** (e.g., `*.png`, `**/*.png`, `assets/*.PNG`, `*.{png,jpg}`) matching the file's extension case-insensitively.
      2. **A specific non-wildcard filename stem/path** (e.g., `assets/logo.png`, `logo.png`, `myExactImage.png`, `report-final.pdf`).
- **Path Separator & Casing Consistency**:
     - Normalized all path separators (`\` to `/`) across include patterns and file paths to adhere to repository standards on Windows and POSIX.
     - Ensured consistent case-insensitive extension matching via `picomatch(patternExt, { nocase: true })`.
- **Test Coverage**: Added comprehensive test cases in `read-many-files.test.ts` covering false-positive rejection (`**/*report*/**` vs `reports/quarterlyreport.png`), explicit binary requests (`assets/logo.png`), path separators (`assets\logo.png`), case-insensitivity (`assets/*.PNG`, `assets/Logo.png`), and unit tests for `isAssetExplicitlyRequested`.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29045

## How to Validate
1. Run unit test suite for `read-many-files`:
     npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/tools/read-many-files.test.ts

prs.title: fix(mcp): request offline access for Google endpoints and preserve clientSecret on refresh
prs.body:
## Summary

Fixes an issue where remote MCP servers configured with OAuth 2.0 against Google endpoints (e.g. Google Workspace APIs such as Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive) or other confidential OAuth providers fail to receive refresh tokens on initial login and fail during background token refresh, trapping users in an hourly re-authentication loop.

## Details

1. **Offline Access & Consent Prompt for Google Endpoints:**
   In `packages/core/src/utils/oauth-flow.ts` (`buildAuthorizationUrl`), when the authorization URL targets Google endpoints (`accounts.google.com` or `*.google.com`), automatically append `access_type=offline` and `prompt=consent` (if not already explicitly provided in the URL). This mirrors the CLI's internal OAuth login in `packages/core/src/code_assist/oauth2.ts` and ensures Google issues a `refresh_token` upon authorization code exchange instead of only a transient 1-hour `access_token`.

2. **`clientSecret` Storage & Propagation on Refresh:**
   When an MCP server's OAuth client is registered with a `client_secret` (as is required by Google for Web/Desktop client applications during token refresh), Google's token endpoint (`https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token`) strictly rejects refresh requests with `client_secret is missing` if the secret is omitted:
   - Added optional `clientSecret?: string` to `OAuthCredentials` (`packages/core/src/mcp/token-storage/types.ts`).
   - Updated `MCPOAuthTokenStorage.saveToken` to accept and preserve `clientSecret` across updates.
   - Updated `MCPOAuthProvider.getValidToken` and `MCPOAuthProvider.getValidTokenWithMetadata` to resolve and forward `clientSecret` to `refreshAccessToken` and persist it on subsequent saves.
   - Updated `getStoredOAuthToken` (`packages/core/src/tools/mcp-client.ts`) to forward `clientSecret` from stored credentials.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29577
Related to #29048

## How to Validate

1. Run unit tests for `oauth-flow`:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/utils/oauth-flow.test.ts
   ```
2. Run unit tests for token storage and provider:
   ```bash
   npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/mcp/oauth-token-storage.test.ts src/mcp/oauth-provider.test.ts

3. Run lint and typecheck:
   ```bash
   npm run typecheck --workspace @google/gemini-cli-core
   npx eslint packages/core/src/utils/oauth-flow.ts packages/core/src/mcp/oauth-token-storage.ts packages/core/src/mcp/oauth-provider.ts packages/core/src/tools/mcp-client.ts

prs.title: fix(cli): persist sandbox authentication and sessions
prs.body:
## Summary

Persist authentication, folder-trust, and session state across sandbox container invocations.

This fixes the repeated authentication prompts, lost sessions, and folder-trust restart loop reported in #29461 while keeping the rest of the host Gemini configuration isolated from the sandbox.

## Details

- Stores sandbox-owned persistent state in `~/.gemini/sandbox`.
- Restores approved state into the isolated settings directory before starting the container.
- Saves approved state before removing the temporary settings directory.
- Uses an explicit allowlist for authentication, trust, history, and session files.
- Persists only the selected authentication fields from `settings.json`; hooks, commands, and other host settings remain excluded.
- Protects the persistent directory and authentication settings with restrictive filesystem permissions.
- Adds unit coverage for restoration, persistence, allowlisting, authentication-setting filtering, and sandbox lifecycle integration.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29461

## How to Validate

Run the focused unit tests:

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- \
  src/utils/sandboxUtils.test.ts \
  src/utils/sandbox.test.ts
```

Run ESLint against the changed files:

```bash
npx eslint --no-cache --max-warnings 0 \
  packages/cli/src/utils/sandbox.ts \
  packages/cli/src/utils/sandbox.test.ts \
  packages/cli/src/utils/sandboxUtils.ts \
  packages/cli/src/utils/sandboxUtils.test.ts
```

For a Docker integration test:

```bash
GEMINI_SANDBOX=docker npm run build:sandbox
GEMINI_SANDBOX=docker npm start -- --sandbox
```

1. Authenticate and trust the working directory.

The local Docker smoke test confirmed that credentials and folder trust were restored without entering the restart loop. A complete live-session interaction was blocked by an unrelated unsupported-nightly-client response, while session persistence paths are covered by the unit tests.

prs.title: fix(core): make mid-stream retry backoff abort-aware
prs.body:
## Summary

Cancelling a request (ESC) during a mid-stream retry did not stop the retry loop in `GeminiChat`: content errors were retried without consulting the abort signal, and the backoff slept on a raw `setTimeout`, so a cancelled request still emitted `RETRY` events and retry telemetry and re-entered `makeApiCallAndProcessStream()` before unwinding. Cancellation now short-circuits immediately.

## Details

- `geminiChat.ts`: gate both retry branches on `!signal.aborted`, and wait with the existing abort-aware `delay(ms, signal)` helper (`utils/delay.ts`) instead of a raw timer. If the signal fires during the backoff, the original error is surfaced without logging a retry failure, matching what the post-loop `signal.aborted` check already does.
- Two regression tests in `geminiChat.test.ts`: a content error after cancellation makes no further API call and no retry telemetry (on `main` it makes 4 calls); an abort during the backoff rejects immediately (on `main` the test times out waiting for the timer).

## Related Issues


Fixes #29716
Fixes #29027

## How to Validate

```
npx vitest run packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.test.ts
npm run preflight
```

Both pass locally (114 tests in that file; full preflight green). Manually: start a streaming request against a flaky endpoint, press ESC while the stream is retrying, and confirm no further `RETRY` events or model calls appear.

prs.title: fix(core): preserve functionResponse parts and functionCall metadata when stripping prefixes (#29589)
prs.body:
## Summary

Preserves all fields of `functionResponse` (such as multimodal `parts`) and `functionCall` (such as `partialArgs` and streaming metadata) when `stripToolCallIdPrefixes()` removes tool name prefixes from IDs.

## Details

In `packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.ts`, `stripToolCallIdPrefixes()` stripped `<toolName>__` prefixes from `functionResponse` and `functionCall` IDs by manually reconstructing objects with hardcoded `{ name, response, id }` and `{ name, args, id }` subsets.

When `read_file` or other tools return multimodal payloads (images, screenshots, inline data), `convertToFunctionResponse` attaches them to `functionResponse.parts` if multimodal tool use is supported. Because `stripToolCallIdPrefixes()` reconstructed `newPart.functionResponse` without `parts`, all binary/image content was discarded prior to sending the request to Gemini / Vertex AI, causing models to hallucinate descriptions of unseen images. Similarly, extra fields on `functionCall` were dropped.

This PR uses object spread (`...fr` and `...fc`) to preserve all existing properties while updating the stripped `id`.

## Related Issues

Closes #29589

## How to Validate

Run unit tests:
```bash
npx vitest run packages/core/src/core/geminiChat.test.ts -t "stripToolCallIdPrefixes"
```

prs.title: docs(sandbox): document that IDE integration is unavailable inside container sandboxes
prs.body:
## Summary

IDE integration (`/ide status`, `/ide enable`, open-file context, native diffs)
does not work when Gemini CLI runs inside a **container sandbox**
(`GEMINI_SANDBOX=docker|podman|runsc|lxc`) while the IDE runs on the host.
The docs currently say the opposite for Docker
(`docs/ide-integration/index.md` › "Using with sandboxing": *"the IDE
integration can still connect to the VS Code extension running on your host
machine"*), which sends users with gVisor/Docker sandboxes down a `/ide install`
rabbit hole. This PR corrects that statement and documents the limitation where
users pick a sandbox method and where they troubleshoot it.

Docs-only; no runtime changes.

## Details

Why the connection cannot succeed on current builds (verified against the code
and with a layer-by-layer `curl` reproduction under both `runc` and `runsc`):

1. **Loopback-only bind** — the companion server listens on `127.0.0.1` only
   (`packages/vscode-ide-companion/src/ide-server.ts`, since #8512). From a
   bridge-networked container, `host.docker.internal` resolves to the
   `host-gateway` IP, so the TCP connection is refused on native Linux.
2. **Host allow-list** — only `localhost:<port>` / `127.0.0.1:<port>` are
   accepted (#8512); `host.docker.internal:<port>` gets `403 Invalid Host
   header` (also reported with `curl` in #13627).
3. **Bearer token** — the companion requires `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_AUTH_TOKEN`, which
   `packages/cli/src/utils/sandbox.ts` deliberately does **not** forward into
   the sandbox (the discovery file in the host tmpdir is not visible either), so
   requests get `401`.

Under gVisor the usual `--network host` workaround for (1) also fails because
netstack's loopback is sandbox-private — that is the only gVisor-specific
delta behind #21331. Making this work requires forwarding the IDE credential
into the sandbox (flagged as a sandbox-escape risk in #29597 / #29653) plus a
new transport, so it is a roadmap-level design change rather than a bug fix;
this PR only makes the docs truthful in the meantime.

Changes:

- `docs/ide-integration/index.md`
  - Replace the incorrect Docker bullet under **Using with sandboxing** with an
    accurate description of the container-sandbox limitation and why it exists.
  - Add a bullet clarifying that dev containers / Remote - SSH (extension host
    and CLI in the same environment) do work.
  - Add a troubleshooting step for the `Failed to connect to IDE companion
    extension` message when running in a container sandbox.
- `docs/cli/sandbox.md`
  - Add a `NOTE` callout in the container-based sandbox section.
  - Add an **IDE integration doesn't connect** entry under Troubleshooting.

## Related Issues

Related to #21331

## How to Validate

1. Read the rendered diff of `docs/ide-integration/index.md` and
   `docs/cli/sandbox.md`; confirm the relative links resolve
   (`../ide-integration/index.md#using-with-sandboxing` and
   `#using-with-sandboxing`).
2. `npx prettier --check docs/cli/sandbox.md docs/ide-integration/index.md`
3. `node scripts/lint.js --sensitive-keywords`
4. Optional behavioural check of the statement being documented, on Linux with
   Docker and the companion extension running in VS Code:
   ```bash
   # from the VS Code integrated terminal
   GEMINI_SANDBOX=docker gemini   # then run /ide status  -> Disconnected
   GEMINI_SANDBOX=runsc  gemini   # then run /ide status  -> Disconnected
   ```

prs.title: fix(core): let /ide enable reconnect after the IDE server restarts
prs.body:
## Summary

After VS Code's **Developer: Reload Window** (or an extension update/disable), the CLI running in the surviving integrated terminal reported `🔴 Disconnected: IDE connection error…`, and `/ide enable` kept failing with `Failed to connect to IDE companion extension…` until VS Code was fully closed and reopened.

#29674 fixed the server side of #28785 (`IdeServer.stop()` hanging and leaking its port file). This PR fixes the **client side**, which could not survive an IDE-server restart even with a fixed extension — and still cannot with the Marketplace extension (v0.20.0), which predates #29674 and leaks a port file on every reload.

Two defects in `IdeClient`:

1. **Discovery tried a single port file.** The reloaded extension host starts a new server (new port, new token, new port file), but the terminal's `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT` / `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_AUTH_TOKEN` stay frozen at the old values. `getConnectionConfigFromFile()` used that frozen port as the tie-breaker, so a leaked old file was selected deterministically, `connect()` never fell through to the live file, and the env fallback pointed at the same dead port.
2. **A superseded client kept driving the state.** `onerror`/`onclose` were bound to the `IdeClient`, not to the client that registered them, and `establish*Connection()` never closed the previous client. After a successful `/ide enable`, the old transport's SSE reconnection attempts against the dead port (1 s, 2.5 s) flipped the state back to `Disconnected` while the new connection was healthy.

Two source files in `packages/core`, no public API change, no new `eslint-disable`.

## Details

### `ide-connection-utils.ts`

- New `getConnectionConfigsFromFile(pid)` returns **every** workspace-valid candidate, best first: the file whose port matches `GEMINI_CLI_IDE_SERVER_PORT` (the window the terminal belongs to), then the rest in the existing `sortConnectionFiles()` order. When no file matches the workspace it still returns the single best-sorted entry so the detailed "Directory mismatch" error is preserved.
- `getConnectionConfigFromFile()` is now `candidates[0]` — the ranking of the preferred file is **unchanged** (all 46 pre-existing tests pass untouched). The three inline config types were replaced by an exported `IdeConnectionConfig` alias. The module is not re-exported from core's index.

### `ide-client.ts`

- `connect()` iterates the candidates, each with **its own** auth token, before the env fallbacks. Behaviour is identical whenever the first candidate answers — the only case that worked before.
- `registerClientHandlers()` captures the client it is registering for; `onerror`/`onclose` no-op once `this.client` has moved on.
- New `retireClient()`, called by both `establishHttpConnection()` and `establishStdioConnection()` before creating a new `Client`: detaches the handlers and `close()`s the superseded client (aborting its socket and retry timers); a rejected `close()` is debug-logged.
- A failed attempt no longer leaves `this.client` pointing at a `Client` that never connected (`dropFailedClient()`, scoped to that attempt's client), so `openDiff`/`closeDiff` fail fast on `!this.client`; failed attempts are debug-logged. (Review feedback.)

### Deliberately out of scope

- Deleting stale files from the client (unsafe when the CLI runs in a sandbox/remote where a port is legitimately unreachable); an extension-side GC of dead sibling files is a natural follow-up.
- Auto-reconnect on disconnect (policy change). Users still see one `IDE connection error… run /ide enable` line after a reload; this PR makes that documented recovery actually work.
- Carried over: a stale file whose port was reused by an unrelated process that accepts TCP but never answers would wait for the SDK's `initialize` timeout (same exposure as before, now per candidate).

## Related Issues

Related to #28785 — client-side follow-up to #29674 (which fixed `IdeServer.stop()`; the issue was closed by it, but the reload symptom it mentions remained).

## How to Validate

**Unit / integration tests**

```bash
npm test -w @google/gemini-cli-core -- src/ide/
# 7 files, 185 passed | 1 skipped
```

- `ide-connection-utils.test.ts` — +9 cases for `getConnectionConfigsFromFile` (legacy file, empty/error paths, workspace filtering and order, env-port promotion with fallbacks retained, no env match, mismatch → single entry, malformed files, singular returns the first candidate).
- `ide-client.test.ts` — +13 cases: candidate iteration (next candidate on failure with its own token, stop at first success, http → stdio candidate, env fallback after all candidates, disconnected when nothing answers), reconnecting (superseded client closed and detached, its late error/close ignored, errors from the current client still reported, rejected `close()` tolerated) and failed attempts (HTTP and stdio failures leave no client behind, `openDiff`/`closeDiff` fail fast, a later successful candidate's client is kept). Also fixes the latent singleton reset in that file (`instancePromise`, not `instance`) so its tests are actually isolated.
- `ide-client.server-restart.test.ts` (new) — real `node:http` MCP servers and real port files in a private `TMPDIR`, no SDK mocks: (1) leaked file matching the frozen env port, (2) late errors from the superseded transport after a clean restart, (3) several leaked files with no env hint, (4) the env-matching window still wins when several servers are alive. (1) and (2) fail on `main` with exactly the user-facing messages above and pass with this change.

**End-to-end with the real `/ide` commands** (harness kept out of the tree): the real `ideCommand()` actions from `packages/cli`, the real `IdeClient`, and the real companion `IDEServer` (vscode API mocked), executed as stash-fix → rebuild → run → restore → rebuild → run:

| Step | `main` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/ide status` | `🟢 Connected` | `🟢 Connected` |
| Reload Window (A: v0.20.0 leaks file · B: fixed extension) | — | — |
| `/ide status` ≈1 s later | `🔴 Disconnected: IDE connection error…` | same (by design, one notification) |
| `/ide enable` | A: `🔴 Disconnected: Failed to connect to IDE companion extension…`  | `🟢 Connected` |
| `/ide status` 4.5 s later | B: `🔴 Disconnected: IDE connection error…` | `🟢 Connected`, `isDiffingEnabled() === true` |

**Manually in VS Code**

1. `rm -f /tmp/gemini/ide/gemini-ide-server-*.json` (macOS: `$TMPDIR/gemini/ide/`), open the repo, run `gemini` in the integrated terminal, `/ide status` → `🟢 Connected to VS Code`.
2. **Developer: Reload Window**; keep the terminal. Within ~1–2 s the CLI prints `IDE connection error… run /ide enable`.
3. `/ide enable` → **before:** `🔴 Disconnected: Failed to connect to IDE companion extension in VS Code…` (with the Marketplace extension; `ls /tmp/gemini/ide/` shows the leaked old file next to the new one) — **after:** `🟢 Connected to VS Code`, and `/ide status` stays connected; diffs work.

## Summary

<!-- Concisely describe what this PR changes and why. Focus on impact and
urgency. -->
Updates `openDiff` in `@google/gemini-cli-core` to deterministically format and quote command-line arguments when spawning external GUI diff editors via `cmd.exe` (`shell: true`) on Windows (`process.platform === 'win32'`). This preserves argument boundaries for file paths containing spaces, embedded quotes, trailing backslashes, or Windows shell metacharacters while keeping POSIX (`linux`, `darwin`) subprocess arguments unchanged.

  - Wraps arguments containing whitespace or shell-significant characters in double quotes (`"..."`), escapes internal double quotes (`"` -> `""`) along with any preceding backslashes, doubles trailing backslashes before the closing quote, and preserves literal percent signs (`%`) inside quotes.
- Updated `openDiff` in `packages/core/src/utils/editor.ts` to map `diffCommand.args` through `quoteCmdArg` exclusively when `process.platform === 'win32'`.
- Added Windows and cross-platform unit tests in `packages/core/src/utils/editor.test.ts` covering `openDiff` and   `quoteCmdArg`.

prs.title: fix(core): respect read-only files and hard links in atomic writeTextFile
prs.body:
## Summary

Since the atomic write in #29499, `StandardFileSystemService.writeTextFile` silently **overwrites read-only files** and **splits hard links**. A rename is permitted by the directory's permissions alone and never consults the destination file's write bit, so a `0444` file that the CLI used to refuse with `EACCES` is now replaced, and the write tool's `PERMISSION_DENIED` branch never fires for it. The same rename gives the path a new inode, so editing one name of a hard link leaves the other names on the old content.

This PR restores both behaviours with two small guards in `writeTextFile`, before the temp file is created:

1. `fs.access(realPath, W_OK)` on an existing destination, so a non-writable file fails with `EACCES` exactly as a plain `fs.writeFile` would.
2. When the destination has more than one hard link (`stat.nlink > 1`), write in place instead of renaming, so every link keeps seeing the same content.

## Details

- **Root cause.** `open(O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC)` checks the *file's* permission bits; `rename(2)` checks only the *directory's*. Swapping one for the other dropped the permission check and the inode identity at the same time.
- **Why `fs.access` rather than re-deriving permissions from `stat.mode`.** `access(W_OK)` is the kernel's own answer and covers ACLs, immutable files (`EPERM`), read-only mounts (`EROFS`) and root (which bypasses mode bits for a plain write too). It is also what Vim's `'readonly'` detection uses.
- **Why in-place for hard links.** This trades atomicity for correctness in that one case, deliberately: a torn read lasts for one write, while a split link stays wrong until somebody notices. Vim's `backupcopy=auto` makes the same call (`nlink > 1` → write in place).
- **Single `stat`.** `getFileMode()` became `statIfExists()` so the mode and the link count come from the one `stat` that was already there; the only new syscall is the `access`.
- **New files are unaffected.** The access check only runs when the destination exists; creation is still governed by the directory's permissions as before.
- **Windows.** A read-only destination was already refused on Windows (`MoveFileEx` fails with `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED` → `EACCES`), but only after `renameWithRetry` burned 5 attempts (~750 ms). It now fails immediately. libuv's `fs.access(W_OK)` reports a read-only file as `EPERM` on Windows, whereas opening it for writing fails with `EACCES` there as everywhere else, so `assertWritable()` rethrows that one case as `EACCES` (with `path`/`syscall`) on `win32` only. POSIX `EPERM` (immutable files) is passed through unchanged, since a plain write fails with `EPERM` there too. This keeps `writeTextFile`'s error contract identical to the pre-#29499 behaviour on every platform.
- No changes to `write-file.ts` or `edit.ts`; the existing `EACCES → PERMISSION_DENIED` mapping simply fires again. No new `eslint-disable` directives.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29721

## How to Validate

### 0. create the file susted by the reporter
gcli_ro.mts
```Typescript
// gcli_ro.mts, at the repository root
import fs from 'node:fs';
import os from 'node:os';
import path from 'node:path';
import { StandardFileSystemService } from './packages/core/src/services/fileSystemService.js';

const dir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'ro-'));
const ro = path.join(dir, 'locked.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(ro, 'original\n');
fs.chmodSync(ro, 0o444);
const a = path.join(dir, 'a.txt'), b = path.join(dir, 'b.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(a, 'shared\n'); fs.linkSync(a, b);

try { fs.writeFileSync(ro, 'plain write\n'); console.log('fs.writeFile on 0444: wrote'); }
catch (e: any) { console.log('fs.writeFile on 0444:', e.code); }

const svc = new StandardFileSystemService();
try { await svc.writeTextFile(ro, 'replaced\n'); console.log('writeTextFile on 0444: wrote, content =', JSON.stringify(fs.readFileSync(ro, 'utf8')), 'mode =', (fs.statSync(ro).mode & 0o777).toString(8)); }
catch (e: any) { console.log('writeTextFile on 0444:', e.code); }

await svc.writeTextFile(a, 'edited\n');
console.log('hard link: a =', JSON.stringify(fs.readFileSync(a, 'utf8')), 'b =', JSON.stringify(fs.readFileSync(b, 'utf8')), 'nlink(a) =', fs.statSync(a).nlink);
```

### 1. Reproduction script from the issue

```bash
# gcli_ro.mts at the repository root (verbatim from the issue)
npx tsx gcli_ro.mts
```

Before (`main` @ 42c518220):

```
fs.writeFile on 0444: EACCES
writeTextFile on 0444: wrote, content = "replaced\n" mode = 444
hard link: a = "edited\n" b = "shared\n" nlink(a) = 1
```

After:

```
fs.writeFile on 0444: EACCES
writeTextFile on 0444: EACCES
hard link: a = "edited\n" b = "edited\n" nlink(a) = 2
```

### 2. Automated tests

```bash
npx vitest run --root packages/core \
  src/services/fileSystemService.test.ts \
  src/services/fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts \
  src/tools/write-file.test.ts \
  src/tools/edit.test.ts
```

Expected: 139 passed (131 before + 8 new). The behavioural tests fail on `main` without the fix:

| Test file | New case | What it pins down |
|---|---|---|
| `fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts` (real FS) | `refuses to overwrite a read-only file` | rejects with `EACCES` on every platform, content untouched, **no temp file created** |
| `fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts` (real FS) | `keeps every hard link pointing at the new content` | both names read the new content, `nlink` stays 2 |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should fail before creating a temp file when the destination is not writable` | `access(W_OK)` is consulted; `writeFile`/`rename` never called |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should report a read-only destination as EACCES on Windows` | libuv's `EPERM` is surfaced as `EACCES` with `path`/`syscall` on `win32` |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should keep EPERM from the write access check on other platforms` | POSIX `EPERM` (immutable file) is not rewritten |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should not check write access when creating a new file` | new files keep the old creation path |
| `fileSystemService.test.ts` (mocked FS) | `should write in place when the destination has multiple hard links` | in-place `writeFile`, no `rename` |
| `write-file.test.ts` (tool-level, real FS) | `should return PERMISSION_DENIED without modifying a read-only file` | the end-to-end symptom from the issue, on all platforms |

The read-only tests are skipped when running as root, since root legitimately bypasses mode bits for a plain write as well.

### 3. Why existing validation missed this

The only `PERMISSION_DENIED` test in `write-file.test.ts` mocked `writeTextFile` to reject with `EACCES`, so it covered the error mapping but never a real read-only destination; `fileSystemService.atomic.test.ts` asserted that `0600` is *preserved* but never that a non-writable file is *refused*; and nothing in the suite created a hard link. The new tool-level test closes that gap on the real filesystem.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed) — no docs describe the atomic-write internals; nothing to update
- [x] Added/updated tests (if needed)
- [x] Noted breaking changes (if any) — none
- [ ] Validated on required platforms/methods:
  - [ ] MacOS
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
    - [ ] Podman
    - [ ] Seatbelt
  - [ ] Windows
    - [ ] npm run
    - [ ] npx
    - [ ] Docker
  - [x] Linux
    - [x] npm run
    - [ ] npx
