prs.title: fix(desktop): drop the Screen Recording assertion when macOS refuses it
prs.body:
Follow-up to #111183, which landed the `app.asar.unpacked` redirect and closed #88468. This is the second commit from #89633, held back there because it could not be verified on that machine.

## What does this PR do?

The redirect gives `get-windows` a helper it can exec. On some machines the helper then runs and still returns nothing.

`screenRecordingPermission: true` reads like a request for the Screen Recording grant. It is an assertion that the grant is already held: get-windows 9.3.0 appends `--no-screen-recording-permission` only when the option is literally `false`, so passing `true` omits the flag and leaves the Swift helper enforcing its own check. When that check fails the helper prints prose to stdout and exits 0, so the module's `parseMac()` throws `Error parsing window data` and no windows come back at all.

Whether the check passes depends on which process TCC holds responsible for the helper, which varies with how the bundle is signed and launched. The same build enumerates on one machine and returns an error on the next.

`openWindowsWithTitleFallback` drops the assertion on exactly the machines where it fails: one call on the working path, and a retry without the claim only after a throw that the claim could have caused. The cost is window titles, never the window list, and the retry never prompts for Screen Recording. A machine that enumerates today takes the first branch and is unchanged.

`titlesGranted` is what came back rather than what was asked for, and `titlesHiddenNote` keys the "titles are hidden" note off it, so a fallback enumeration explains its own empty titles instead of looking broken. `enumerateWindowsFrontToBack` now answers with that pair; the HUD overlay watch unwraps the windows and is otherwise untouched.

## Credit

@b-rightstart diagnosed the assertion semantics and proposed this shape on #89633.

## Verification, and its limit

Eight new tests: the retry fires and returns windows, the working path stays a single call with titles intact, no retry when titles were never asked for, nothing asserted off macOS, both causes reported when the retry fails too, and the note keyed on the grant rather than the request.

Neither I nor @b-rightstart can execute the retry path: macOS accepts the assertion on both our machines, so these tests are the only coverage here. Anyone who hit `Error parsing window data` after #111183 is the one who can confirm it end to end.

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `vitest electron/window-below.test.ts` | 26 passed |
| `tsc -p tsconfig.electron.json` | clean |
| `eslint` on the three files | 0 errors (4 pre-existing warnings, identical on `main`) |

prs.title: feat(desktop): discover local MCP servers and enable per profile
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

Adds **Find MCP servers / Refresh** and a per-candidate enable switch to the existing Desktop MCP panel. Users can reuse an MCP already configured in another local profile/client, or discover a local HTTP MCP, without manually copying JSON/YAML/TOML. This is explicit copying into one selected profile, **not profile inheritance**.

## Related work

Searched existing issues/PRs for MCP discovery, import, scan and local auto-discovery. The merged #87572 supports paste-based import; this complements that flow with host-side discovery and explicit activation. Existing startup tool-discovery fixes do not provide this setup flow.

## Type of change

- [x] New feature

## Changes

- Read raw definitions from Hermes profiles, Claude Code (including configured project entries), Cursor, the platform's Claude Desktop config location, and **Codex user-level `config.toml`** (`~/.codex/config.toml`, or `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml`). Do not launch stdio programs, install packages or read `.env`/token stores during discovery.
- Translate Codex stdio/HTTP settings into Hermes configuration: command/args/cwd, environment references, HTTP headers, bearer-token variable references, timeouts and tool filters. Preserve Codex's deny-after-allow tool policy, including empty allowlists and literal tool names. Unsupported policies/helpers are listed as unavailable instead of silently discarded.
- Probe loopback listeners reported by `psutil` at `/mcp` and `/sse`; require a valid MCP initialize response. Use bounded concurrency, response size and cancellation deadlines covering slow headers as well as bodies; bypass proxies/redirects and clean up allocated HTTP sessions.
- Return candidate metadata, never the full configuration. Inline credentials make a candidate unavailable; preserve non-secret settings, tool filters and environment references.
- Re-read/fingerprint the source on explicit connect, reject name collisions or stale candidates, and save through the canonical profile-scoped config owner. Enable a disabled source when the user explicitly connects it. Codex fingerprints cover the raw entry before translation, so changes to settings omitted during conversion also invalidate the candidate.
- Route the renderer request to the selected connection/profile, guard stale profile responses, reuse the configured-server list and existing reload flow, and translate the discovery UI in all six locales.
- Document the scope and limitations.

## How to test

1. Configure a non-secret stdio MCP in a source profile, leaving another profile empty. For Codex, add a `[mcp_servers.<name>]` entry to the user-level `config.toml`.
2. In Desktop, select the target profile, open Capabilities → MCP and choose Find MCP servers.
3. Confirm the source candidate is listed (with a **Codex** source label for Codex entries), then switch it on. It appears in the configured list; only the target config changes and the existing MCP reload flow runs.
4. Change a source after discovery or introduce a target name collision: connect must refuse without overwriting. Try an inline credential: it must not be disclosed or copied.

### Verification performed on Linux/WSL — original implementation

These results belong to the original implementation at `2d1d833`; they have **not** been rerun after the Codex follow-up.

- `scripts/run_tests.sh` over discovery, MCP config, probe redaction, dashboard admin endpoints, profile unification and reload-all-sessions: **173 passed, 0 failed** (6 files).
- Desktop Vitest: discovery component/API routing and existing MCP import/server helpers: **29 passed** (4 files).
- Desktop TypeScript `tsc -p . --noEmit`: passed.
- ESLint on touched Desktop files, Ruff on backend files, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Real Camofox browser → discovery React component → authenticated FastAPI routes → isolated target config: passed. The scan also found an actual local HTTP MCP via initialize. Checked destination/source/default files after the switch; an unauthenticated discovery request returned 401. This is an isolated component/preload harness, **not a packaged Electron acceptance run**, and the stdio fixture tested configuration transfer rather than native tool execution.
- Regression proven RED/GREEN for a server trickling HTTP headers past the nominal timeout.

### Codex follow-up verification (`00b0f1f`)

- **55 tests passed** with `PYTHONPATH=. python -m pytest -q tests/hermes_cli/test_mcp_discovery_codex.py -k 'not integration'` in an isolated checkout of the changed Python modules plus the unchanged `mcp_security.py`. Covers conversion, filter semantics, invalid/unsupported settings, `CODEX_HOME`, and real bounded TOML file reads.
- Python compilation passed.
- Added **8 backend integration cases** covering authenticated discovery/connect, target isolation, raw-source changes, deletion, collisions, inline credentials, custom Codex home, and malformed TOML alongside healthy clients. **Not executed in this environment**; they require the full repository/backend dependencies.
- Full backend, lint, Desktop and packaged Electron checks were **not rerun** for this follow-up. No frontend code changed.

### Intentional limits

Not an exhaustive computer-wide inventory: custom paths, HTTPS-only/authenticated endpoints, legacy GET-only SSE, non-loopback bindings and other OS/network namespaces (including Windows-host listeners from WSL) may need manual setup. Discovery runs on the selected gateway. Environment references require credentials in the destination; secrets are not transferred. Candidate metadata expires after five minutes. No installed Hermes checkout or live bot config was modified.

Codex discovery is limited to its **user-level config**. Project `.codex/config.toml` layers, plugin manifests, remote execution environments and credential stores are not enumerated. Explicit OAuth configuration uses Hermes's own authentication flow; Codex tokens are not migrated. Unsupported approval/required-server policies or credential helpers require manual configuration rather than a lossy import.

## Checklist

- [x] Read contribution guidance; searched existing work.
- [x] Scope limited to the requested feature; focused tests and documentation added.
- [x] Cross-platform config paths and namespace limitations considered.
- [ ] Full repository test suite (not run; focused matrix above).
- [ ] Codex backend integration cases on the full repository (not run).
- [ ] Packaged Desktop smoke test on macOS/Windows (not run).

prs.title: fix(cron): scoped worker waits out an update's gateway handover instead of failing
prs.body:
## What does this PR do?

During `hermes update`, the new code is installed before the running gateway is replaced. If a cron job fires in that window, the old gateway's ticker spawns a restart-safe external worker, and that worker runs the new code. The worker finds its own parent gateway as the owner, sees it as an older runtime it isn't allowed to stop, and books the run as FAILED:

```
GatewayUnavailableError: Gateway incompatible: runtime_protocol (an older Hermes gateway owns this profile and was not verified; run: hermes gateway stop)
```

The suggested remedy doesn't fit either: the caller is a child of that gateway, and the update restarts the gateway anyway.

With this change, the worker waits for the replacement gateway instead of failing. This follows the rule `cron/scheduler_gateway_gate.py` already applies to headless ticks: a slot lost to a restart window is a missed fire, not a job failure.

The wait is deliberately narrow. `incompatible/runtime_protocol` is also used for a newer owner, a foreign install and an unverified or recycled pid, and a plain `draining` or `starting` can mean an operator drain or a hung owner. So the fix doesn't retry on those. It adds a structured reason for the one case that is known to resolve itself:

- `replace_incompatible_owner` now reports `owner_is_parent` when the owner pid is this process's parent, instead of folding it into `owner_unverified`.
- `ensure_gateway_runtime` maps that to `incompatible` with `reason_code="parent_outdated"`.
- `GatewayUnavailableError` carries the `reason_code`.

The worker waits only when all of these hold:

- the verdict is `incompatible/parent_outdated` or `draining/update_paused` (the update fence);
- the process is the external worker for this execution, and it was dispatched as `scoped`, which is the only mode that survives the gateway restart;
- nothing has been submitted yet, and the job hasn't been cancelled.

The wait is capped at 900 s. Execution progress is touched while it waits. Cancellation and the deadline are checked before every dial, and when the wait ends without a ready gateway, the original error is raised as before. Interactive callers, `degraded` workers and in-process dispatch (Windows/macOS) still fail fast.

## Related Issue

Refs #134889 (report: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/134889#issuecomment-6182345464), a follow-up to #106742.

## Type of Change

- [x] 🐛 Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## Changes Made

- `hermes_cli/gateway_runtime_replace.py`: new `owner_is_parent` refusal with its own detail text.
- `hermes_cli/gateway_runtime.py`: `owner_is_parent` → `incompatible` / `parent_outdated`.
- `hermes_cli/gateway_client.py`: `GatewayUnavailableError` keeps the discovery `reason_code`.
- `cron/scheduler_worker_env.py`, `cron/scheduler.py`: the worker env records the dispatch mode (`_HERMES_CRON_WORKER_DISPATCH`).
- `cron/scheduler_owner_handover.py` (new): the bounded wait. `cron/scheduler_authority.py` dials through it.
- `cron/AGENTS.md`: one line on the rule.
- Tests: `tests/cron/test_cron_owner_handover.py`, `tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_runtime_parent_owner.py`.

## How to Test

1. `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/cron/test_cron_owner_handover.py tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_runtime_parent_owner.py`
   - A confirmed handover waits, then runs on the new gateway.
   - Every other refusal fails fast: a newer owner, a foreign install, an unverified owner, an operator drain, and a starting deadline.
   - An interactive caller fails fast.
   - A cancel during the wait submits nothing.
   - The wait stops at its bound.
   - A parent owner is never stopped, and is reported as `parent_outdated`.
2. `scripts/run_tests.sh tests/cron/ tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_runtime*.py tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway_client*.py`

## Checklist

### Code

- [x] I've read the Contributing Guide
- [x] My commit messages follow Conventional Commits
- [x] I searched for existing PRs to make sure this isn't a duplicate
- [x] My PR contains only changes related to this fix
- [ ] I've run `pytest tests/ -q` and all tests pass. I ran the cron and gateway-runtime suites, not the whole suite. Two tests there fail on this host as root, and they fail the same way on unmodified `main`: `test_gateway_runtime_ensure.py::test_reserved_profile_without_pid_or_control_is_never_absent` and `test_gateway_runtime_service.py::test_ensure_checks_effective_service_binding_before_start[default-deadline]`. For the first, `chmod(0)` doesn't deny access to UID 0.
- [x] Code health (`scripts.code_health --base upstream/main`) and ruff pass
- [x] I've added tests for my changes
- [x] I've tested on my platform: Ubuntu (Linux 7.0, aarch64)

### Documentation & Housekeeping

- [x] I've updated `AGENTS.md` (`cron/AGENTS.md`)
- [x] Config keys: N/A
- [x] Cross-platform: Windows and macOS dispatch cron in-process, so they keep the current fail-fast behaviour
- [x] Tool descriptions/schemas: N/A

prs.title: fix(openai_compat): echo Gemini thought_signature in extra_content
prs.body:
## 📝 Description

Fix the `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT` error returned by Gemini 3 when continuing a tool-calling conversation through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint:

```
Function call is missing a thought_signature in functionCall parts.
This is required for tools to work correctly, and missing thought_signature
may lead to degraded model performance. ... https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thought-signatures
```

Gemini 3 requires the `thought_signature` to be **echoed back inside `extra_content.google.thought_signature`** on every `functionCall` part of the request history. PicoClaw's OpenAI-compatible provider only sent it under `function.thought_signature`, which Gemini rejects on the follow-up request.

Two distinct bugs are fixed:

1. **Serialization** (`pkg/providers/common/common.go`): resolve the signature from every known location (`Function.ThoughtSignature`, top-level `ThoughtSignature`, `ExtraContent.Google`) and emit it inside `extra_content.google.thought_signature`. A signature-less tool call no longer emits an empty `extra_content` block.

2. **Streaming capture** (`pkg/providers/openai_compat/provider.go`): `parseStreamResponse` did **not** read the `thought_signature` at all. Since `ChatStream` is the default chat path, any tool call produced in streaming mode lost the signature entirely, so the next request was rejected. The delta parser now captures the signature from both `function.thought_signature` and `extra_content.google.thought_signature`.

## 🗣️ Type of Change
- [x] 🐞 Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] ✨ New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)
- [ ] 📖 Documentation update
- [ ] ⚡ Code refactoring (no functional changes, no api changes)

## 🤖 AI Code Generation
- [ ] 🤖 Fully AI-generated (100% AI, 0% Human)
- [x] 🛠️ Mostly AI-generated (AI draft, Human verified/modified)
- [ ] 👨‍💻 Mostly Human-written (Human lead, AI assisted or none)

## 🔗 Related Issue

Refs #3230, Refs #3111 — same `400` on OpenAI-compat Gemini 3 tool loops.

## 📚 Technical Context (Skip for Docs)
- **Reference URL:** https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thought-signatures
- **Reasoning:**
  - Gemini 3 (via both `generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/` and gateways such as Cloudflare AI Gateway) mandatory-signature contract. The signature must be resent on the assistant tool-call message of the following request, and Google specifically looks for `extra_content.google.thought_signature`.
  - `extra_content` is a Google-only extension. Providers that don't support it ignore unknown fields on the assistant tool-call object, so emitting it is additive; the `google` key is what only Gemini accepts. This mirrors upstream's existing `serializeToolCalls` behavior of preserving signatures, ordering the resolution so a top-level `ThoughtSignature` (set by the streaming path) still wins.

## 🧪 Test Environment
- **Hardware:** PC (linux/amd64)
- **OS:** Linux
- **Model/Provider:** `gemini-3.8-flash` via Google AI Studio OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai/`)
- **Channels:** Telegram / web

## 📸 Evidence (Optional)
<details>
<summary>Click to view Logs/Screenshots</summary>

Reproduced failure mode (provider fallback from a DeepSeek primary to Gemini):

```
failover(format): provider=openai model=gemini-3.8-flash status=400
Function call is missing a thought_signature in functionCall parts...
```

Local verification:
```
$ go test ./pkg/providers/...
ok  github.com/sipeed/picoclaw/pkg/providers/common        0.032s
ok  github.com/sipeed/picoclaw/pkg/providers/openai_compat 0.121s
(... all pkg/providers packages pass)

$ golangci-lint run --build-tags goolm,stdjson ./pkg/providers/...
0 issues.
```

New tests cover: wire payload contains `"extra_content":{"google":{"thought_signature":"..."}}` when the signature is only on `Function`, only top-level, or only on `ExtraContent`; no `extra_content` when there is no signature; and a streaming `ChatStream` round that captures the signature from the delta.

</details>

## ☑️ Checklist
- [x] My code/docs follow the style of this project.
- [x] I have performed a self-review of my own changes.
- [x] I have updated the documentation accordingly. (inline doc comments; no user-facing docs affected)

issues.title: fix(setup/onecli): restrict OneCLI admin API and Postgres to loopback after install

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Maintainer-set

labels.name: PR: Fix
labels.description: Bug fix

issues.body:
## Summary

On bare-metal Linux, OneCLI's installer auto-detects the `docker0` bridge IP and binds all three of its published ports to it — including the admin API (`:10254`) and Postgres (`:5432`), not just the proxy gateway (`:10255`). Because NanoClaw runs agent containers on that same bridge by design, every agent container can reach the unauthenticated admin API and Postgres without any misconfiguration on the operator's part.

From any NanoClaw agent container:

```
$ curl http://172.17.0.1:10254/api/agents
HTTP 200 — returns every agent's access token, no auth required

$ (echo > /dev/tcp/172.17.0.1/5432) && echo "postgres reachable"
postgres reachable  (default creds: onecli/onecli)
```

This is tracked upstream at **onecli/onecli#268**.

## Proposed fix

Add a `hardenOneCliBinds()` step to `setup/onecli.ts` that runs after the OneCLI installer completes. It rewrites `~/.onecli/docker-compose.yml` to pin `:10254` (admin API) and `:5432` (Postgres) to `127.0.0.1`, while leaving `:10255` (proxy gateway) on the bridge IP so agent containers can still reach it. Then restarts the OneCLI containers to apply.

- **Idempotent** — a marker comment prevents double-patching on setup re-runs
- **Fail-safe** — if the compose layout doesn't match the expected pattern (i.e. OneCLI changed their file), logs a warning and skips rather than silently mangling the file
- **`--reuse` mode** — does not rewrite; detects the unsafe bind and emits a warning instead
- Adds `HARDENED` + `HARDEN_NOTE` fields to `status.json` so it's observable

## Scope

~80–100 lines including vitest unit tests covering: vanilla compose patched correctly, already-patched no-op, unknown layout no-op-with-warning, missing file no-op-with-warning.

## Related

- Upstream issue: https://github.com/onecli/onecli/issues/268
- Upstream auth hardening issue: https://github.com/onecli/onecli/issues/263

prs.title: fix(update-skills): attribute a barrel import to the skill that appends it
prs.body:
<!-- contributing-guide: v1 -->
## Type of Change

- [ ] **Feature skill** - adds a channel or integration (source code changes + SKILL.md)
- [ ] **Utility skill** - adds a standalone tool (code files in `.claude/skills/<name>/`, no source changes)
- [ ] **Operational/container skill** - adds a workflow or agent skill (SKILL.md only, no source changes)
- [x] **Fix** - bug fix or security fix to source code
- [ ] **Simplification** - reduces or simplifies source code
- [ ] **Documentation** - docs, README, or CONTRIBUTING changes only

## Description

**What** — `detectInstalledSkills` attributes a channel-barrel import to the skill that actually appends it, instead of assuming every import has its own `add-<name>` skill.

**Why** — `/add-slack` appends two imports to `src/channels/index.ts`: `slack.js` and its `slack-a2a-guard.js` companion. Detection maps each one to `add-<name>`, so the refresh looks for a skill that does not exist and fails:

```
Missing .claude/skills/add-slack-a2a-guard/SKILL.md
```

`refreshInstalledSkills` treats that as a failed skill, which blocks `/update-nanoclaw` validation on any install with Slack. I hit this on a routine update.

**How it works** — ownership is read from the skills' own `nc:append to:src/channels/index.ts` directives: an import a skill declares belongs to that skill, and a skill owning several imports is refreshed once under its own name. An unclaimed import still maps to `add-<name>`, so a channel installed without a skill is still reported — the missing-skill check keeps its point. A `SKILL.md` that fails to parse simply claims nothing; refresh reports the parse failure itself with a better message than detection could.

**How it was tested** — two cases added to `scripts/update-skills.test.ts`: the companion case (asserts one entry, not two) and an unclaimed import (asserts `add-<name>` attribution still happens). I verified the companion test fails on `main` and passes with the fix. Full file green (6/6), `tsc --noEmit` clean, and the real update that surfaced this now validates end to end.

prs.body:
<!-- nanoclaw-pr-template:v2 -->

## Summary

Moves agent containers to the latest Claude Code, Agent SDK and Codex. These versions make Claude Haiku 5.5 the default Haiku model.

- **Claude Code 2.1.296 and Agent SDK 0.3.296:** from 2.1.293, Claude Haiku 5.5 is Claude Code's default Haiku model on the Anthropic API. Claude Code's background requests and groups set to `haiku` move from Haiku 4.5 to Haiku 5.5, which costs $0.10/$0.50 per Mtok against $1/$5.
- **Codex 0.162.1:** from 0.161, Codex's default model is GPT-6.1 Sol. Codex groups with no model set start new threads on it; existing threads keep the model they started on.
- **Pins:**

prs.title: fix(add-dashboard): read transcripts without loading whole files
prs.body:
<!-- nanoclaw-pr-template:v2 -->

## Summary

Keeps the `/add-dashboard` pusher working when an agent's transcript gets large.

- **Problem**: the pusher reads transcripts with `fs.readFileSync(…, 'utf-8')`. Past ~512 MB (Node's maximum string length) that throws `Cannot create a string longer than 0x1fffffe8 characters`. `collectContextWindows` doesn't catch it and `collectSnapshot` uses `Promise.all`, so the whole snapshot fails: the dashboard stops updating and the error is logged every minute. `scanJsonlTokens` catches it and silently drops the file from token totals.
- **Why a normal install hits it**: the agent-runner rotates transcripts at 12 MB, but only when a container starts. A busy agent's container is never idle long enough to be restarted. We saw one container run ~9.5 h on a single long task, with image tool results, and its transcript reached 540 MB.
- **Also below the limit**: every 60 s the pusher re-read every transcript of every agent from byte 0. That costs CPU and memory in proportion to the whole history.
- **Fix**: files are never read whole any more.
  - Context window: read the transcript's last 256 KB, doubling the window until a usage line is found.
  - Token totals: a per-file cache of `{ inode, offset, entries }`. Each snapshot reads only the appended bytes, in 1 MB chunks, and holds a half-written last line until it is complete. A file that shrank or was replaced is read again; files that disappear are dropped from the cache.
  - Log backfill: read the last 512 KB of `nanoclaw.log` for the 200 lines.
  - A transcript that vanishes between the directory walk and the read (e.g. rotated away) is skipped, not the whole snapshot.
- **Same output**: on a 100 MB transcript the snapshot's `context_windows` and `tokens` are identical before and after.
- **Trade-off**: the token entries now stay in memory between snapshots (one small object per assistant call) instead of being rebuilt every minute.
- **Out of scope**: which transcript counts as "live" (the newest `.jsonl`, which can be a subagent's), and when the agent-runner rotates transcripts.

<details>
<summary>Before / after numbers</summary>

A fake data dir with one transcript of 200 KB tool-result lines plus an assistant usage line after each. One snapshot through `startDashboard()` (vitest), peak RSS from `/usr/bin/time -v`.

| Transcript | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 100 MB | snapshot in 626 ms, peak RSS 456 MB | 234 ms, 155 MB, identical snapshot |
| 600 MB | **no snapshot** (error at start and again at 60 s), peak RSS 1.17 GB | 1.06 s, 158 MB; totals correct (3,139 requests) |

Later snapshots read only the bytes appended since the previous one.
</details>

## Related work

No issue: this is a self-contained fix inside `.claude/skills/add-dashboard/resources/`, with its tests. #3417 also edits `dashboard-pusher.ts` (shutdown wiring, SQL, docs); its hunks don't overlap these lines.

## Change kind

- [x] `kind/bug`
- [ ] `kind/feature`
- [ ] `kind/documentation`
- [ ] `kind/cleanup`
- [ ] `kind/hardening`

## Validation

- New tests in `dashboard-pusher.test.ts`, driven through `startDashboard()` like the existing one:
  - `finds the last usage line behind a long tail, without reading the transcript whole`
  - `reads only appended bytes, and counts a half-written line once it is complete`
  - `starts over when a transcript is replaced by a smaller one`
  - `still posts the snapshot when a transcript vanishes mid-read`
- Same tests on the old pusher -> 3 of the 4 fail (the "replaced" test guards the new cache, so it passes on both).
- Fresh clone, skill applied per `SKILL.md` steps 1–3 -> `pnpm run build` OK -> `pnpm exec vitest run src/dashboard-pusher.test.ts src/dashboard-wiring.test.ts` -> 7 passed.
- Same clone: `pnpm exec tsc --noEmit` -> OK; `prettier --check` on the changed files -> OK.
- Same clone: `pnpm exec vitest run` -> 3569 passed, 1 failed: `src/group-skills.test.ts` › "resolves the legacy shape to the same anchored result as the segments form", which also fails on untouched `main` in our environment.
- Manual: 600 MB transcript -> see the numbers above.
- [x] Tests cover the changed behavior (or Validation says why not)

- [x] User-visible change — release note below


prs.title: fix(delivery): carry a mime type on outbound files so Teams accepts them
prs.body:
## Type of Change

- [ ] **Feature skill** - adds a channel or integration (source code changes + SKILL.md)
- [ ] **Utility skill** - adds a standalone tool (code files in `.claude/skills/<name>/`, no source changes)
- [ ] **Operational/container skill** - adds a workflow or agent skill (SKILL.md only, no source changes)
- [x] **Fix** - bug fix or security fix to source code
- [ ] **Simplification** - reduces or simplifies source code
- [ ] **Documentation** - docs, README, or CONTRIBUTING changes only

## Description

**What** — adds an optional `mimeType` to `OutboundFile`, derives it from the filename extension where the outbox is read, and stops the chat-sdk bridge dropping it on the way to the adapter.

**Why** — an agent that produces an image can't deliver it on Teams. Every `send_file` with a PNG fails, and the agent is never told: `send_file` reports success as soon as the row is written, and the failure happens later on the host's delivery poll. From the agent's side the file simply never arrives.

`OutboundFile` carried only `{ filename, data }`, and the bridge forwarded exactly those two fields. `@chat-adapter/teams` then does:

```js
const mimeType = file.mimeType || "application/octet-stream";
const dataUri = bufferToDataUri(buffer, mimeType);
```

so a PNG goes out as `contentUrl: "data:application/octet-stream;base64,..."` and Teams rejects the whole activity with `400 Bad Request`.

Worth stating explicitly, because it's the tempting reading for a 133KB image: **this is not the size limit.** Teams answers oversize with `413`/`MessageSizeTooBig`, and base64 image payloads are [explicitly excluded](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/bots/how-to/format-your-bot-messages) from its 100KB activity budget. A 400 is the content type.

**How it works** — `mimeForFilename()` in `attachment-naming.ts`, called from `readOutboxFiles()`; the bridge forwards the field in both of its file-upload paths. `EXT_TO_MIME` is derived from the existing `MIME_TO_EXT` rather than written out a second time, with a round-trip test, so the inbound and outbound tables can't drift.

It returns `undefined` for unrecognized extensions rather than guessing `application/octet-stream`. Adapters already have that fallback, and handing them a guess dressed as a fact is what caused this.

**How it was tested** — typecheck clean and 84 tests green on this branch standing alone on `main`. Then on a live install: the same PNG that had failed three times with a 400 delivered on the first retry after the fix — `Message delivered ... channelType="teams" fileCount=1`, outbox cleared, no error.

## Related

- #1988 fixes the same class of bug one adapter down, with an extension→mimetype map inside `src/channels/whatsapp.ts`. This addresses it once at the shared seam instead, which covers Teams and every other adapter that has to declare a content type — and would make that local map redundant. Happy to rebase around whichever you'd rather land first.
- Touches `src/session-manager.ts` and `src/host-core.test.ts`, which #3505 also moves — likely a small conflict depending on merge order.

prs.title: test(setup): give the spawn-based mailbox checks a realistic timeout
prs.body:
## Type of Change

- [ ] **Feature skill** - adds a channel or integration (source code changes + SKILL.md)
- [ ] **Utility skill** - adds a standalone tool (code files in `.claude/skills/<name>/`, no source changes)
- [ ] **Operational/container skill** - adds a workflow or agent skill (SKILL.md only, no source changes)
- [x] **Fix** - bug fix or security fix to source code
- [ ] **Simplification** - reduces or simplifies source code
- [ ] **Documentation** - docs, README, or CONTRIBUTING changes only

## Description

**What** — gives the three cases in `setup/mailbox-compatibility.test.ts` a 60s timeout instead of vitest's 5s default.

**Why** — each case spawns a Node process that transforms the TypeScript graph through tsx on a cold cache. Measured at **4.96s running the file alone**, which leaves nothing at all for a loaded machine:

```
FAIL  setup/mailbox-compatibility.test.ts > standalone setup mailbox composition >
      setup/register.ts loads with the default mailbox composition
Error: Test timed out in 5000ms.
```

It passes every time the file is run on its own and fails in a full-suite run, which presents as flake rather than as the slow-by-construction test it is.

On the update path it's worse than noise: `/update-nanoclaw` runs the full suite in its staging worktree and refuses cutover on any failure, so a slower machine can block a legitimate update on this alone. That's how I hit it.

**How it works** — a named `SPAWN_TIMEOUT_MS` constant passed as the timeout argument to `it.each` and `it`, with a comment recording the measurement so the number isn't mistaken for an arbitrary bump. No production code touched.

**How it was tested** — `pnpm exec vitest run setup/mailbox-compatibility.test.ts` → 3 passed. Full suite green in a run that previously failed on this file.

prs.body:
## Type of Change

## Description

Card-click authorization and Chat SDK sender resolution both decide whether a
platform user id is "already namespaced" with `payload.userId.includes(':')`.
That holds for the ids most adapters emit, but **Teams user ids natively
contain a colon** (`29:1Eiqnrl…`). They are read as already-prefixed and left
bare, so they never match the stored `teams:29:1Eiqnrl…`.

Two observable consequences on any Teams install:

1. **No Teams user can approve anything.** Every card click is rejected as an
   unauthorized clicker — channel registration, unknown-sender approval, and
   the generic approval path. The log shows the mismatch plainly:

   ```
   Channel registration click rejected — unauthorized clicker
     clickerId="29:1Eiqnrl…"  expectedApprover="teams:29:1Eiqnrl…"
   ```

2. **A duplicate user row accumulates.** The Chat SDK bridge projects
   `author.userId` raw into `senderId`, so an inbound Teams sender resolves to
   a bare `29:…` row rather than the `teams:29:…` one holding their roles. The
   owner arrives unprivileged; messaging still works when `sender_scope=all`,
   which is what makes it easy to miss.

### Approach

Adds `namespacedUserId(channel, raw)` in `src/platform-id.ts`, testing
`startsWith(`${channel}:`)` instead of `includes(':')`, and uses it at the
three click-authorization sites plus the bridge's sender projection.

Two deliberate choices:

- **Not reusing `namespacedPlatformId`.** Its `@`/`+` escapes would stop
  prefixing WhatsApp JIDs and Signal phone numbers, silently changing those
  channels. The new helper has no escapes, so the only ids whose treatment
  changes are colon-bearing ones without a channel prefix.
- **Fixing the bridge rather than `extractAndUpsertUser`.** Changing the
  resolver would alter how *every* channel treats colon-bearing handles, and
  its own tests pin the current semantics (`senderId: 'tg:stranger'` asserting
  it stays bare). Namespacing at the projection leaves that contract intact:
  adapters whose ids carry no colon were prefixed by the resolver before and
  are prefixed here now, reaching the same id.

### Testing

Full host suite passes. Verified end to end against a live Teams install:
card clicks now authorize, and the sender resolves to the namespaced identity
holding the `owner` role instead of creating a second row.

prs.title: fix(container): bypass the gateway proxy for host-local addresses so HTTP MCP servers work
prs.body:
## Type of Change

- [ ] **Feature skill**
- [ ] **Utility skill**
- [ ] **Operational/container skill**
- [x] **Fix**
- [ ] **Simplification**
- [ ] **Documentation**

## Description

With a gateway provider active, an HTTP MCP server on `host.docker.internal`
is unreachable from the agent — **and fails silently**.

The gateway injects `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` so all agent egress is
credential-injected. That proxy cannot serve a request aimed at the Docker host
itself: it accepts the connection and closes it. The SDK's MCP handshake
therefore fails, the server is registered, and **none of its tools load** —
with no error in the agent log.

What that looks like in practice: the agent insists it has no access to tools
that `ncl groups config get` shows correctly configured, while a direct `curl`
to the same URL from the same container returns HTTP 200. The only difference
is the proxy env, which makes it easy to "rule out" with a probe that does not
reproduce the agent's environment.

```
# inside a live agent container
curl -X POST http://host.docker.internal:8001/mcp …
  → curl: (52) Empty reply from server

no_proxy=host.docker.internal curl -X POST http://host.docker.internal:8001/mcp …
  → HTTP 200
```

This matters because `ncl groups config add-mcp-server` **explicitly permits**
plain HTTP for `localhost` and `host.docker.internal` (`src/container-config.ts`
rejects plain HTTP for everything else), so those URLs are a documented
configuration that could not work while a gateway is active.

### Approach

Sets `no_proxy`/`NO_PROXY` to `host.docker.internal,localhost,127.0.0.1` in the
agent image. `no_proxy` matches on the **target** host, so this exempts only
host-local traffic; calls to `api.anthropic.com` and every other external host
still route through the gateway and still get their credentials injected. No
change to the egress model.

### Open question for reviewers

Baking this into the Dockerfile is the blunt fix. It may be cleaner for the
gateway provider to emit `NO_PROXY` alongside the proxy vars it already
contributes (`src/gateway-providers/onecli.ts`), so the bypass lives with the
thing that introduces the proxy and non-gateway installs are unaffected. Happy
to move it there — I went with the image because it is provider-agnostic, but I
do not have strong grounds to prefer it.

### Testing

Verified on a live install: before, four HTTP MCP servers registered and zero
tools loaded; after rebuilding the image, the agent calls them successfully.

prs.title: feat(slack): show the task lifecycle as reactions
prs.body:
# feat(slack): show the task lifecycle as reactions

**Branch:** `feat/slack-status-reactions`
**Base:** `main`
**Title:** `feat(slack): show the task lifecycle as reactions`

## What changed

Adds Slack status reactions: the message that triggers a turn gets a reaction that
follows the task through `accepted`, `running`, and `done` or `failed`.

```
 docs/en/configuration.md  |  25 ++++
 docs/zh/configuration.md  |  20 +++
 src/channels/root.zig     |  27 +++++
 src/channels/slack.zig    | 248 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/channels/telegram.zig |  10 +-
 src/config.zig            |  43 +++++++
 src/config_types.zig      |  16 +++
 src/daemon.zig            |  42 ++++++-
 8 files changed, 424 insertions(+), 7 deletions(-)
```

- `src/channels/root.zig`: new `Channel.TaskReaction` enum (`accepted`, `running`,
  `done`, `failed`), new `TaskReactionUpdate` payload, and a new vtable field
  `setTaskReaction` defaulting to `defaultSetTaskReaction`, which returns
  `error.NotSupported`. The default lets the daemon name a lifecycle state on any
  channel without every existing channel file changing.
- `src/channels/slack.zig`: `SlackChannel.setTaskReaction` plus the pure
  `planTaskReaction` transition table, the target parser `slackChannelIdOf`, the
  `reactions.add` / `reactions.remove` request builder, and the vtable wiring
  (`vtableSetTaskReaction`). The account latches `reactions_disabled` on an auth
  failure.
- `src/channels/telegram.zig`: `pub const TaskReaction` becomes an alias for
  `root.Channel.TaskReaction`. No other Telegram change.
- `src/config_types.zig`: `SlackReactionEmojisConfig` and the two new optional
  `SlackConfig` fields.
- `src/config.zig`: parsing tests for the defaults and for an explicit config.
- `src/daemon.zig`: `setInboundTaskReaction` helper, called from
  `processInboundMessage` on the accepted, running, and every terminal path.
- `docs/en/configuration.md`, `docs/zh/configuration.md`: the two new keys, a
  "Slack status reactions" section, and a config example, per the CONTRIBUTING
  rule that user-facing changes update docs in the same PR.

## Why it changed

`status_reactions` and `reaction_emojis` existed only under
`channels.telegram.accounts.<id>`, and the code that drives them is Telegram's
inherent `setTaskReaction`, which is called from the Telegram polling loop. Slack
does not run that loop: it receives events through its own socket/HTTP event
pipeline, so there was no place in the Slack path for the lifecycle to attach to,
and the same config keys would have been dead for Slack.

Copying the Telegram lifecycle into Slack would have forked the state machine into
a second implementation that can drift from the first. Instead the daemon names
the state and the channel keeps the mapping, which is the pattern AGENTS.md
prescribes: extension work implements vtable structs and registers them, it does
not add cross-cutting branches per channel.

## Design notes

### The vtable hook

`Channel.setTaskReaction(update: TaskReactionUpdate)` is a new function-pointer
field on `Channel.VTable`, following the same shape as the existing `setReaction`
and `markRead` hooks. The default implementation returns `error.NotSupported`, so:

- a channel that does not implement the hook is not a compile error and not a
  silent no-op either; the caller gets an explicit error it can ignore,
- the daemon can call the hook unconditionally and let the channel decide.

`setInboundTaskReaction` in `src/daemon.zig` swallows exactly `error.NotSupported`
and logs anything else at debug level. Telegram's vtable is not touched by this
change, so the hook is a no-op for Telegram and its polling-loop lifecycle keeps
running exactly as before.

`Channel.TaskReaction` is the shared vocabulary because the states themselves are
domain-neutral. `telegram.TaskReaction` becomes an alias for it rather than a
duplicate enum, so Telegram's existing call sites and tests keep compiling.

### Where the states are emitted

`processInboundMessage` emits the same sequence the Telegram loop uses, through
the `setInboundTaskReaction` helper:

| State | Emitted |
|---|---|
| `accepted` | after the routing decision returns something other than `.skip`, before the processing indicator |
| `running` | immediately before `processMessageStreaming` |
| `done` | on the draft-edit path and on the normal publish path, after the outbound event is published |
| `failed` | on the streaming error, the draft send failure, the publish failure, and the `makeOutbound` failure |

Every terminal path sets a final state, so a turn does not leave a stale
`accepted` or `running` reaction behind. The helper returns without calling the
channel when there is no message id to react to.

### Why the state to reaction mapping stays channel-local

The daemon passes a state name; each channel resolves it against its own config.
That split is deliberate:

- the value domain differs per channel. Telegram takes emoji characters
  (`TelegramReactionEmojisConfig` defaults to `👀 ⚡ 👍 💔`), Slack takes reaction
  short names (`eyes`, `hourglass_flowing_sand`, `white_check_mark`, `x`). The two
  are not interchangeable, which is why `SlackReactionEmojisConfig` is its own
  struct and only the enum is shared,
- the transport differs. Slack needs a remove-then-add plan, Telegram does not,
- the config type lives next to the channel config it parses, so a new channel
  adds a hook implementation without the daemon learning anything about reactions.

### Add, not replace

Slack reactions accumulate on a message. Adding `white_check_mark` after `eyes`
leaves both, so a transition has to remove the state it is leaving before adding
the state it is entering. `planTaskReaction` returns a `ReactionPlan` of up to two
removals and one add:

| New state | Supersedes | Default plan |
|---|---|---|
| `accepted` | none | add `eyes` |
| `running` | `accepted` | remove `eyes`, add `hourglass_flowing_sand` |
| `done` | `accepted`, `running` | remove `eyes`, remove `hourglass_flowing_sand`, add `white_check_mark` |
| `failed` | `accepted`, `running` | remove `eyes`, remove `hourglass_flowing_sand`, add `x` |

Two properties fall out of the same table:

- **Zero extra calls when two states share a name.** If the name being added
  equals a superseded state's name, that removal is skipped, so the reaction
  already on the message stays put. Setting `accepted` and `running` to
  `hourglass_flowing_sand` makes the `running` transition one add and zero
  removals.
- **An empty name withdraws the state.** `reactionEmoji` maps an empty string to
  null, which drops that state's add and still removes the superseded occurrence.
  With every name empty the plan is empty and no API call is made at all.

Duplicate removals are collapsed, so the plan never issues the same remove twice.

`planTaskReaction` is a pure function, which is what makes the transition table
testable without a network.

### Error handling

`already_reacted` and `no_reaction` are treated as success, so a retry or a
double transition is harmless. Any code matched by the existing
`SlackChannel.isAuthFailureCode` (which already covers `missing_scope`) latches
`reactions_disabled` and logs one warning per account; later turns skip the calls
entirely. Reaction failures never propagate: `setTaskReaction` is best-effort and
returns `void`, so a reaction problem cannot fail a turn.

## Config surface

Two optional keys on the Slack alias, mirroring Telegram's key names:

| Key | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.status_reactions` | bool | `false` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.accepted` | string | `eyes` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.running` | string | `hourglass_flowing_sand` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.done` | string | `white_check_mark` |
| `channels.slack.accounts.<alias>.reaction_emojis.failed` | string | `x` |

Values are Slack reaction short names, not the emoji themselves. An empty string
withdraws the reaction for that state.

```json
{
  "channels": {
    "slack": {
      "accounts": {
        "<alias>": {
          "bot_token": "YOUR_BOT_TOKEN",
          "status_reactions": true,
          "reaction_emojis": {
            "accepted": "hourglass_flowing_sand",
            "running": "hourglass_flowing_sand",
            "done": "",
            "failed": "warning"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The app needs the `reactions:write` scope. Without it the API answers
`missing_scope`, which is logged once and then disabled for that account.

## Backward compatibility

- Both keys are optional and default to the pre-change behavior. With
  `status_reactions` false (the default), `setTaskReaction` returns before
  building a plan or touching the network, so existing Slack deployments are
  unaffected.
- The new vtable field carries a default (`&defaultSetTaskReaction`), so no
  existing channel implementation has to change.
- Telegram's vtable is untouched and `telegram.TaskReaction` still names the same
  enum, so Telegram behavior and its tests are unchanged.
- No config migration is needed.

## Rollback

The change is one commit. `git revert <sha>` restores the previous behavior;
because both keys are optional and default to off, nothing has to be undone in a
config file.

## Security impact

- The only new outbound requests are `reactions.add` and `reactions.remove` on
  the Slack Web API. Both require `reactions:write` and nothing else; no other
  scope, endpoint, file, or shell surface is added. The scope is only exercised
  when `status_reactions` is explicitly enabled.
- The request body is built with the existing `appendJsonStringW` escaper, so the
  channel id, timestamp, and reaction name are JSON-escaped rather than
  interpolated.
- No secret is logged. The failure path logs the endpoint name, the API error
  code, and the account alias. The bot token is not included.
- The reaction target comes from the inbound message's own channel and timestamp,
  so no new destination is derived from user input. `slackChannelIdOf` drops the
  thread suffix because Slack keys reactions by channel.

## Validation

Required by CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md for a code change:

```sh
zig build test --summary all   # 0 failures, 0 leaks
zig fmt --check src/           # .githooks/pre-commit
```

`zig build test --summary all` also runs from `.githooks/pre-push`. The pinned
toolchain is Zig 0.16.0 exactly.

No Zig 0.16.0 toolchain was available in the environment where this PR body was
prepared, so those two commands are reported here as the checks that gate the
change rather than as output. No test or format result is claimed that was not
observed; CI results will be added once they are available.

What the branch does cover without a network:

- `src/channels/slack.zig` adds 6 tests: the default transition table including
  the explicit removals, the shared-name case (0 removals on the `running`
  transition), the all-empty no-op case, the target parser, the inert path when
  `status_reactions` is off, and the vtable wiring. `callSlackApi` is stubbed
  under `builtin.is_test`, so none of these tests perform network I/O.
- `src/config.zig` adds 2 tests: defaults when the keys are absent, and an
  explicit config, both with the allocations freed.
- The existing `Channel message operations default to not supported` test in
  `src/channels/root.zig` gains an assertion that `setTaskReaction` returns
  `error.NotSupported` on the default vtable.

Manual check for a reviewer with a Slack app that has `reactions:write`: enable
`status_reactions`, send a message that triggers a turn, and watch the reaction
move through the configured names and disappear when `done` is set to an empty
string. That path is not covered by the automated tests.

## Notes

- Only the message that triggered the turn is reacted to. The agent's own reply is
  not, and no reaction is placed on a parent message.
- Reaction names are passed through to the API as configured. An unknown name
  comes back as an API error code, which `callSlackApi` logs; it does not affect
  the turn and does not disable reactions.
- Telegram still runs its own polling-loop lifecycle. A later change could point
  Telegram's vtable at the shared hook and delete the duplicate, but that is a
  separate concern and is not attempted here.

prs.title: fix(providers): route configured providers by explicit prefix
prs.body:
# PR title

fix(providers): route configured providers by explicit prefix

# Branch

fix/route-providers-by-prefix

# PR body

## What changed

An explicit `provider/model` model reference previously resolved only for the primary provider and for providers listed in `reliability.fallback_providers`. A provider that is configured under `models.providers` but is not a fallback target was never registered as a routing target, so `/model <provider-alias>/<model-id>` was unusable for it. This PR makes every configured provider reachable by its explicit prefix, without adding it to the failover chain.

Two files:

- `src/providers/reliable.zig`: new `routable` field on `ReliableProvider` (defaults to `&.{}`, so the struct stays backward compatible), a `withRoutable()` builder next to the existing `withExtras()` / `withModelFallbacks()`, and the explicit-prefix matching extracted into a shared `matchExplicitProviders()` helper that is applied to `extras` and to `routable` with the same longest-prefix accounting. The exact-provider-name branch of `resolveProviderTarget()` consults `routable` (lookup order: `extras`, then `routable`, then the primary provider). `deinit()` and `warmup()` now cover the new slice.
- `src/providers/runtime_bundle.zig`: new `collectRoutableProviderNames()` collects every provider configured under `models.providers` except the default provider (already the primary) and providers already covered by `reliability.fallback_providers` (name comparison via `provider_names.providerNamesMatch`, duplicates skipped). The extra-slot arrays are sized as `reliability.fallback_providers.len + rotating_key_count + routable.len`, and the single entry array is split back into two slices at wiring time: `entries[0..failover_entry_count]` goes to `withExtras()`, `entries[failover_entry_count..]` goes to `withRoutable()`. When the inner provider is the provider router, no routable entries are built, since the router already resolves explicit refs against the same provider set.

## Why it changed

Concrete failure, all names placeholders:

1. `models.providers` contains the default provider `<primary-provider>` and a second provider `<provider-alias>` whose `base_url` points at a gateway that serves `<model-id>`.
2. `reliability.fallback_providers` is empty, or lists a different provider. The user runs `/model <provider-alias>/<model-id>`.
3. `RuntimeProviderBundle.init()` registered only `reliability.fallback_providers` (plus rotated keys) as `ReliableProvider` extras, so `<provider-alias>` had no entry anywhere in the wrapper.
4. `resolveProviderTarget()` found no explicit-prefix match, fell through to the bare-model path, stripped the `<provider-alias>/` prefix, and sent `<model-id>` to the primary provider.
5. `<primary-provider>` does not serve `<model-id>` and rejects the request with `Model <model-id> is not allowed`.

The prefix was parsed correctly the whole time. The only defect was that the provider it named was never registered as a routable target, which also explains why the workaround was to add the provider to `reliability.fallback_providers` even when it was not wanted as a failover target.

## Routing and failover stay separate

This is the part worth reviewing closely. `routable` is not a second failover chain:

- `extras` still contains exactly `reliability.fallback_providers` plus rotated keys, in configured order. Nothing was added to it, and `withExtras()` receives the same bounds as before (`entries[0..failover_entry_count]`).
- `routable` entries are consulted only in the explicit-prefix paths: longest-prefix matching against both the configured entry name and the provider runtime name, plus the exact `provider/model` name lookup in `resolveProviderTarget()`. A bare model never consults them.
- A bare model (`<model-id>` with no prefix) therefore keeps its existing behavior: it goes to the primary provider, and on failure it fails over through the configured `fallback_providers` only. A configured-but-not-fallback provider is never used as a failover target.
- The regression test `ReliableProvider keeps failover limited to extras` pins this: the primary fails, the configured fallback serves the request, and the routable-only provider is asserted to have received zero calls.

## Validation

Not run locally: the authoring environment has no Zig 0.16.0 toolchain, so there is no local test output to paste. CI is expected to provide the pass/fail evidence. The checks this branch must pass, per `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `.githooks`:

- `zig build test --summary all` (required for code changes; 0 failures, 0 leaks)
- `zig fmt --check src/` (what `.githooks/pre-commit` runs)
- Optional, as this is not a release-sensitive change: `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall`

Tests added or updated here (4 new, 1 updated):

- `ReliableProvider routes an explicit prefix to a non-failover provider` (new, `reliable.zig`): the prefixed reference reaches the routable provider, that provider receives the bare model id, and the primary is not called.
- `ReliableProvider keeps failover limited to extras` (new, `reliable.zig`): bare-model failover behavior is unchanged.
- `ReliableProvider resolves supportsStreamingNativeTools through an explicit prefix` (updated, `reliable.zig`): now exercises a routable entry instead of an extra.
- `RuntimeProviderBundle makes non-fallback configured providers routable` (new, `runtime_bundle.zig`): for a config whose second provider is not a fallback target, `extras.len == 0` and `routable.len == 1`.
- `RuntimeProviderBundle keeps fallback providers in the failover chain` (new, `runtime_bundle.zig`): the fallback target stays in `extras` while the other configured provider lands in `routable`.

Each new test carries a comment naming the regression it guards, per `AGENTS.md` 8.1.

## Notes

- No config surface change: no new keys, no changed defaults, no new CLI flags. The only new state is internal (`routable`), derived from the existing `models.providers` and `reliability.fallback_providers`.
- Backward compatible: existing configurations keep identical behavior for bare models and for failover. The only behavior change is that an explicit `provider/model` reference to a configured provider now resolves instead of being stripped and rejected by the primary provider.
- Rollback: `git revert` of the squash commit. No migration, no persisted state, nothing written to disk.
- Docs: this restores behavior that `docs/en/commands.md` already documents (`/model <provider/model>` pins the session to that model). No config key or flag text changes, so no doc edit is strictly required; if maintainers want it explicit, the clarification belongs in that `/model` bullet.
- Ownership: routable entries are appended to the same `reliable_entries` / `extra_holders` arrays the bundle already owns and frees, so deinit stays in one place. The collected name slice borrows from `cfg.providers`, which outlives the bundle, and is freed by `init()` once the entries are built.
- Risk tier: medium per `AGENTS.md` 5 (`src/providers/**` behavior change, no boundary or security impact).
- Linked issue: <ISSUE-URL>

prs.title: feat(config): add agent.reasoning_mode default
prs.body:
# feat(config): add agent.reasoning_mode default

- Branch: `feat/configurable-reasoning-default`
- Scope: one concern, a configurable default for the `/reasoning` display mode
- Risk tier (AGENTS.md §5): high, config schema. Change is additive only, no security, runtime, or gateway boundary is touched.
- Breaking change: no

## Summary

Adds the optional `agent.reasoning_mode` key (`off` | `on` | `stream`, default `off`) to the `agent` config section. It sets the reasoning display mode applied to newly created sessions, and it becomes the value `/restart` and `/debug reset` restore instead of the hard-coded `off`.

Diffstat (8 files, 182 insertions, 14 deletions):

```text
 docs/en/configuration.md | 18 ++++++++++
 docs/zh/configuration.md | 18 ++++++++++
 src/agent/commands.zig   |  2 +-
 src/agent/root.zig       | 49 +++++++++++++++++++--------
 src/config.zig           | 72 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/config_mutator.zig   |  1 +
 src/config_parse.zig     |  5 +++
 src/config_types.zig     | 31 +++++++++++++++++
 8 files changed, 182 insertions(+), 14 deletions(-)
```

## What changed

### `src/config_types.zig` (+31)

- New `pub const ReasoningMode` enum with variants `off`, `on`, `stream`, plus `toSlice()` and a case-insensitive `fromSlice()`.
- New field `AgentConfig.reasoning_mode: ReasoningMode = .off`.
- The enum is declared in the config layer so a parsed value can be assigned to the runtime field with no conversion step.

### `src/config_parse.zig` (+5)

- `parseJson` reads `agent.reasoning_mode`. A non-string value or an unrecognized string returns `error.InvalidReasoningMode`, so a typo fails loudly instead of silently falling back to `off`.

### `src/config.zig` (+72)

- `Config.save()` emits `reasoning_mode` inside the pretty-printed `agent` section, so a saved config round-trips through `parseJson`.
- New tests: `parse agent.reasoning_mode`, `agent.reasoning_mode defaults to off`, `agent.reasoning_mode rejects invalid values`, `Config.save preserves agent.reasoning_mode`.

### `src/config_mutator.zig` (+1)

- `pathRequiresRestart` returns true for `agent.reasoning_mode`, alongside the existing `agent.default_queue_mode` entry. This matches the documented behavior that new sessions pick the value up after a restart.

### `src/agent/root.zig` (+36 / -13)

- Deletes the private `ReasoningMode` enum and aliases `config_types.ReasoningMode`, removing the conversion that would otherwise be needed when applying the configured value.
- New field `default_reasoning_mode: ReasoningMode = .off`, documented as the value restored by `/restart` and `/debug reset`.
- `Agent.fromConfig` sets both `reasoning_mode` and `default_reasoning_mode` from `cfg.agent.reasoning_mode`.
- New test `Agent.fromConfig applies agent.reasoning_mode and resets to it` covers the configured default, a per-session `/reasoning on` override, and the reset path, and carries a `Regression:` comment citing the idle-eviction problem.

### `src/agent/commands.zig` (+1 / -1)

- `resetRuntimeCommandState` sets `self.reasoning_mode = self.default_reasoning_mode` instead of `.off`. This is the shared code path behind `/restart` and `/debug reset`, so one change fixes both commands.

### `docs/en/configuration.md` (+18) and `docs/zh/configuration.md` (+18)

- New `agent.reasoning_mode` section in both languages, placed next to the other `agent.*` keys. CONTRIBUTING requires syncing English and Chinese pages when both audiences are affected, and this is a user-facing config key, so both pages are updated in this PR to satisfy that requirement.

## Why it changed

`reasoning_mode` always started at `off`, and `resetRuntimeCommandState` hard-coded `.off` for `/restart` and `/debug reset`. Sessions are evicted after `agent.session_idle_timeout_secs`, so anyone who wants reasoning visible had to re-run `/reasoning on` after every idle eviction.

The display mode is a preference, not per-session state, so it belongs in the `agent` config section. `agent.default_queue_mode` already solves the same class of problem for the queue mode, so this follows an existing pattern rather than introducing a new one. This also gives the new key a concrete caller in `Agent.fromConfig` and `resetRuntimeCommandState`, as required by AGENTS.md §3.2.

`/reasoning <mode>` still overrides the mode for the current session. The config key only changes what a new or reset session starts from.

## Validation

No local Zig toolchain was available when this patch was written. The commands below were not executed locally and no results are claimed here. CI is the source of truth for this PR.

Required for code changes (CONTRIBUTING, AGENTS.md §8), with Zig 0.16.0:

```bash
zig build test --summary all      # must be 0 failures and 0 leaks
zig fmt --check src/              # the same check .githooks/pre-commit runs
```

Optional release check, since the change touches config and agent paths:

```bash
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSmall
```

Test coverage added by this PR (AGENTS.md §8.1), 5 tests total:

- `src/config.zig`: `parse agent.reasoning_mode`, `agent.reasoning_mode defaults to off`, `agent.reasoning_mode rejects invalid values`, `Config.save preserves agent.reasoning_mode`
- `src/agent/root.zig`: `Agent.fromConfig applies agent.reasoning_mode and resets to it`

## Config surface

- Key: `agent.reasoning_mode`
- Type: string enum, one of `off`, `on`, `stream` (case-insensitive)
- Default: `off`
- Optional: yes. A config that does not set the key behaves exactly as it does today.

```json
{
  "agent": {
    "reasoning_mode": "stream"
  }
}
```

- `off` hides reasoning content, `on` prints a `Reasoning:` quote block above the final reply, `stream` prints reasoning live while the model produces it.
- `/reasoning <off|on|stream>` overrides the mode for the current session only.
- Changes apply to sessions created after a restart. `config_mutator.pathRequiresRestart` reports this for `nullclaw config set`.

## Risks and follow-up work

- Risk: a config typo now fails config loading instead of being ignored. This is intentional (AGENTS.md §3.4 fail fast) and matches how `agent.default_queue_mode` already behaves.
- Risk: `ReasoningMode` moves from `src/agent/root.zig` to `src/config_types.zig`. Both are internal to the module; no public API is exported and no caller outside these files references the type.
- Follow-up, deliberately not in this PR to keep it single-concern: `resetRuntimeCommandState` also resets `verbose_level` and `usage_mode` to fixed values, which could get the same configurable-default treatment.

## Breaking change

No. The key is optional and defaults to `off`, which is the pre-change behavior for both the initial mode and the reset path. No existing key changes meaning, no CLI flag is removed, and no config file needs editing.

## Rollback

- `git revert` the commit, or
- set `agent.reasoning_mode` back to `off` (or remove the key) and restart. Sessions then behave exactly as they did before this change.

## Notes

- The reset path and the config default now read the same field, so there is a single source of truth for "what mode does a new session start in".
- `/reasoning` command parsing is unchanged. Only the initial value and the reset value moved.
- No new dependency and no new allocation on the hot path. The addition to `Agent` is one small enum field next to the existing `reasoning_mode`.
- No secrets, tokens, or personal data are included in the code, tests, docs, or this description.
